From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

The **Nigeria Atomic Energy Commission** is the agency responsible for the coordination of [research and development](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_and_development "Research and development") activities for the use of atomic and nuclear energy in Nigeria.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

NAEC was established in 1976.[[2]](#cite_note-2) NAEC partners with the [Federal Ministry of Power](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Ministry_of_Power_(Nigeria) "Federal Ministry of Power (Nigeria)").[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)

In May 2024, it announced a partnership with Centre for Energy Research and Training to build a nuclear reactor for power generation.[[5]](#cite_note-5) In May 2025, Adebayo Adelabu, the federal minister of power of Nigeria, disapproved of NAEC's plan for four 1,200-megawatt nuclear plants, instead suggesting modular reactors that fit Nigeria's decentralized power model.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

In April 2025, [Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea_Hydro_&_Nuclear_Power "Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power") (KHNP) signed a [memorandum of understanding](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorandum_of_understanding "Memorandum of understanding") (MOU) with NAEC to expand nuclear cooperation in Africa.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Contents of https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-65737846:
29 May 2023

![](https://static.files.bbci.co.uk/bbcdotcom/web/20260714-093448-684066af18-web-3.14.0-3/grey-placeholder.png)![Reuters Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu waves at a crowd, during his swearing-in ceremony in Abuja, Nigeria May 29, 2023](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/6144/production/_129900942_02b44f9d81a2ac4e75b186bb9c249ab37a17ddfd281_182_4579_25771000x563.jpg.webp)Reuters

Bola Tinubu won February's election with 37% of the vote, a victory that is being challenged in court

**The new president of Africa's largest democracy, Nigeria, has used his inaugural address to make a major policy announcement to ease pressure on government finances.**

Bola Tinubu said the decades-long subsidy on petroleum products was being scrapped.

"Fuel subsidy is gone," he told a packed crowd in the capital, Abuja.

He won disputed elections with a promise to renew hope - but he faces tough economic and security challenges.

It is not clear when the new policy will kick in, but ending the subsidy will lead to a rise in the price of petrol and could have a knock on effect on other prices.

Previous Nigerian governments have tried and failed to end the subsidy that was first introduced in the 1970s.

Despite its oil wealth, Nigeria is unable to refine enough crude to meet local demands so it imports petroleum products, which are then sold at a government-set price.

But the subsidy is a huge drain on public finances. Last year it gulped 4.3trn naira ($9.3bn; £7.5bn) and for the first half of this year, 3.36trn naira was budgeted for it.

The new president said the subsidy could no longer be justified and that the funds would instead be spent on public infrastructure and to improve the lives of people.

Mr Tinubu, 71, takes over from Muhammadu Buhari, who has stepped down at the end of his two terms.

He is under pressure to tackle the economic crisis.

Inflation is running at its highest rate for nearly 18 years, one in three people are unemployed and the output of the vital oil industry is shrinking.

Mr Tinubu acknowledged these challenges in his speech, saying his team would release its economic roadmap in the coming weeks but pointed out that interest rates were too high.

* [The five tests awaiting Nigeria's new president](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-africa-65719385)

He won the election in February with 37% of the vote. His main rival Atiku Abubakar polled 29%, and Labour's Peter Obi 25%.

Mr Tinubu's victory is being challenged in court by the two opposition candidates.

They say the outcome was manipulated.

But Mr Tinubu said he was "spreading his hand across the political divide", and described the election as hard-fought and of a better quality than previous ones.

He also said that women and young people would feature prominently in his administration and hinted at employing more security personnel to tackle the security crisis, which includes kidnappings for ransom.

As a former governor of Lagos, he revitalised Nigeria's commercial hub - no easy job - and his allies say he will take the same technocratic and thoughtful approach to running the vast country of more than 200 million people.

But opponents of the new president say he has lost the vitality he used to forcefully modernise Lagos.

Since the election he has travelled abroad twice, raising questions about his health. In 2021 he spent months in London being treated for an undisclosed illness.

He has brushed off the criticism, saying the job does not require the fitness of an Olympic athlete - and his associates are quick to remind everyone that US President Joe Biden is older, at 80.

But if Mr Abubakar and Mr Obi have their way then Mr Tinubu may not be in power for very long.

The election tribunal is expected to start hearing the main arguments in their case on Tuesday and a ruling should be given within the next six months.

Contents of https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-67227814:
26 October 2023

Chris Ewokor & Wedaeli ChibelushiBBC News, Abuja & London

![](https://static.files.bbci.co.uk/bbcdotcom/web/20260714-093448-684066af18-web-3.14.0-3/grey-placeholder.png)![AFP Nigeria President Bola Tinubu arrives for the closing session of the New Global Financial Pact Summit, on June 23, 2023 in Paris.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/B89C/production/_131006274_bola2.jpg.webp)AFP

Bola Tinubu was elected with 37% of votes cast in a three-way race

**Nigeria's Supreme Court has thrown out both opposition challenges to President Bola Tinubu's election win.**

The two main opposition candidates had sought to reverse February's presidential election, alleging it was marred by irregularities.

The Election Petition Court upheld Mr Tinubu's victory last month, but the opposition insisted Nigeria's highest court should quash the judgement.

A presidential election result has never been overturned in Nigeria.

In a unanimous decision, a panel of seven justices first dismissed the challenge by Atiku Abubakar, who came second in the poll, and then rejected a similar one from Peter Obi, who came third.

"It is my view that there is no merit in this appeal and it is hereby dismissed," said Justice John Inyang Okoro of the case made by Mr Abubakar's Peoples Democratic Party.

The election was the most fiercely contested since the end of military rule in 1999, with three strong candidates for the first time. Mr Tinubu won with 37% of votes cast, against 29% for Mr Abubakar and 25% for Mr Obi.

With the challenge to his victory finally put to rest, President Tinubu is now expected to focus on how to pull the country out of its current economic crisis.

Nigeria is currently battling a cost-of-living crisis following the removal of a massive fuel subsidy - a situation that has pushed many Nigerians into multi-dimensional poverty.

On 26 July 2023, a [coup d'état](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coup_d'état "Coup d'état") occurred in [Niger](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niger "Niger") when the country's presidential guard detained President [Mohamed Bazoum](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Bazoum "Mohamed Bazoum"), and Presidential Guard commander [General](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_officer "General officer") [Abdourahamane Tchiani](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdourahamane_Tchiani "Abdourahamane Tchiani") proclaimed himself the leader of a new military [junta](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Council_for_the_Safeguard_of_the_Homeland "National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland"), shortly after confirming the coup a success.[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[13]](#cite_note-13)[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-ajtchiani-15)

This was the fifth military coup d'état since the country gained independence from [France](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") in 1960, and the first since [2010](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Nigerien_coup_d'état "2010 Nigerien coup d'état").[[16]](#cite_note-16) The coup was condemned by the [United States](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and [France](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), and by the West African regional bloc [ECOWAS](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECOWAS "ECOWAS"), the latter of which threatened military intervention against the junta, leading to the [2023–2024 Niger crisis](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerien_crisis_(2023–2024) "Nigerien crisis (2023–2024)").[[17]](#cite_note-17)

Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_Nigeria:
Fula_people "Fula people") gunmen at a [police checkpoint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_checkpoint "Police checkpoint") in [Zangon Kataf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zangon_Kataf "Zangon Kataf"), [Kaduna State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaduna_State "Kaduna State").[[7]](#cite_note-7)
* 18 March – [2023 Nigerian gubernatorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Nigerian_gubernatorial_elections "2023 Nigerian gubernatorial elections") and [state of assembly election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Nigerian_state_legislative_elections "2023 Nigerian state legislative elections") are held.[[8]](#cite_note-THISDAYLIVE_–_Truth_and_Reason_2023-8)
* 15–16 March – [At least 100 people are killed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Mangu_violence "2023 Mangu violence") in [Mangu LGA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mangu,_Nigeria "Mangu, Nigeria"), [Plateau State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plateau_State "Plateau State").
* 16 March – An [ambush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Anambra_ambush "2023 Anambra ambush") kills four members of a [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") convoy in [Anambra State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anambra_State "Anambra State").[[9]](#cite_note-9)
* May 2023 – [Hilda Baci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilda_Baci "Hilda Baci") breaks the world record for the longest cooking marathon by an individual, cooking for 93 hours and 11 minutes from May 11 to May 15, 2023. She surpassed the previous record of 87 hours and 45 minutes.[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11)
* 13 June – [Kwara boat disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwara_boat_disaster "Kwara boat disaster"): At least 100 people are killed when a [wedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wedding "Wedding") boat [capsizes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capsize "Capsize") on the [Niger River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niger_River "Niger River") in [Kwara State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwara_State "Kwara State").[[12]](#cite_note-12)
* 7 July – Health officers confirm an outbreak of [diphtheria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diphtheria "Diphtheria") in the capital [Abuja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abuja "Abuja") following the death of a four-year-old. According to NCDC, nearly 800 cases of the disease have been confirmed in the country as of 30 June.[[13]](#cite_note-13)
* 4 September – The 13-kilometre-long (8.1-mile) [Lagos Rail Mass Transit Blue Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagos_Rail_Mass_Transit_Blue_Line "Lagos Rail Mass Transit Blue Line") [rapid transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_transit "Rapid transit") system begins service in Lagos, after being delayed since 1983.[[14]](#cite_note-14)
* Sept 2023 – [Christopher Olusa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Olusa?action=edit&redlink=1 "Christopher Olusa (page does not exist)") breaks the world record for the longest speech marathon, speaking continuously for 112 hours.[[15]](#cite_note-15)[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18)
* 2 October – At least 18 people are killed in an explosion at an illegal [oil refinery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_refinery "Oil refinery") in [Emohua district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emohua_Town "Emohua Town"), Rivers State.[[19]](#cite_note-19)
* 20 October – Two children were killed and two others injured when a mechanical issue causes a boat engine to catch fire. The incident occurred [Katcha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katcha,_Nigeria "Katcha, Nigeria"), [Niger State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niger_State "Niger State").[[20]](#cite_note-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21)
* 29 October – Seventeen bodies are found, and 73 other people were missing when a boat carrying traders returning from a fish market capsizes on the [Benue River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benue_River "Benue River"). The boat had over 100 passengers on board, 14 of whom are rescued.[[22]](#cite_note-22)
* 30 October – [2023 Yobe State attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Yobe_State_attacks "2023 Yobe State attacks"): At least seventeen people are killed in [Gurokayeya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurokayeya,_Nigeria?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gurokayeya, Nigeria (page does not exist)"), [Yobe State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yobe_State "Yobe State") when [Boko Haram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boko_Haram "Boko Haram")-aligned gunmen storm the village, attacking residents with explosives and firearms when they reportedly refuse to a pay a tax to the [terrorists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrorist "Terrorist").[[23]](#cite_note-23)[[24]](#cite_note-24)
* 31 October – At least 20 people are killed when a [land mine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_mine "Land mine") placed by Boko Haram explodes while they return from the burials of victims from the previous day's shooting.[[25]](#cite_note-25)[[26]](#cite_note-26)
* 6 November – Two people are killed and two others injured when a [tanker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tank_truck "Tank truck") explodes outside the [High Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_commissioner_(Commonwealth) "High commissioner (Commonwealth)") of [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada") in [Abuja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abuja "Abuja").[[27]](#cite_note-27)
* 16 November:
  + Clashes with police and members of the [Islamic Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_Movement_(Nigeria) "Islamic Movement (Nigeria)") during a [pro-Palestine protest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_war_protests "Gaza war protests") leave one dead and several injured in Kaduna.[[28]](#cite_note-28)
  + A boat accident in [Shioro LGA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shioro,_Nigeria?action=edit&redlink=1 "Shioro, Nigeria (page does not exist)"), [Niger State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niger_State "Niger State"), kills at least ten people. 24 others were rescued from the scene.[[29]](#cite_note-29)
* 21 November – At least 25 people are killed and about 200 were injured in a [vehicle crash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vehicle_crash "Vehicle crash") on the Yawuri Expressway in [Magama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magama,_Nigeria "Magama, Nigeria"), Niger State.[[30]](#cite_note-30)[[31]](#cite_note-31)
* 3 December – [Tudun Biri drone strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tudun_Biri_drone_strike "Tudun Biri drone strike"): A [drone strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_strike "Drone strike") on a village in Kaduna State mistakenly kills 85 [civilians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civilian "Civilian").
* 13 December – Four [soldiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_Army "Nigerian Army") and two civilian drivers are killed and two [South Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea") workers are [kidnapped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidnapping "Kidnapping") in an [ambush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambush "Ambush") against a convoy in [Rivers State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rivers_State "Rivers State").[[32]](#cite_note-32)
* 23–25 December - [Nigerian bandit conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_bandit_conflict "Nigerian bandit conflict"): [2023 Plateau State massacres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Plateau_State_massacres "2023 Plateau State massacres")

* 9 January – [Peace Anyiam-Osigwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_Anyiam-Osigwe "Peace Anyiam-Osigwe"), 53, filmmaker and entertainment executive.[[33]](#cite_note-33)
* 14 January – [Femi Ogunrombi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Femi_Ogunrombi "Femi Ogunrombi"), actor and ethnomusicologist.[[34]](#cite_note-34)
* 19 January – [Oladipo Ogunlesi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oladipo_Ogunlesi "Oladipo Ogunlesi"), 99, professor of medicine.[[35]](#cite_note-35)
* 1 February – [Dan Suleiman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Suleiman "Dan Suleiman"), 80, politician, [governor of Plateau State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_governors_of_Plateau_State "List of governors of Plateau State") (1976–1978).[[36]](#cite_note-36)
* 12 September – [MohBad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MohBad "MohBad"), 27, musician.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]
* 20 October – [Alhaji Mansur Nuhu Bamalli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alhaji_Mansur_Nuhu_Bamalli?action=edit&redlink=1 "Alhaji Mansur Nuhu Bamalli (page does not exist)"), 42, Nigerian ambassador to [Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morocco "Morocco").[[37]](#cite_note-37)
* 8 November – [Aderonke Kale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aderonke_Kale "Aderonke Kale"), 84, Nigerian army physicist and first female major-general in the [Nigerian Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_Army "Nigerian Army").[[38]](#cite_note-38)

Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tudun_Biri_drone_strike:
From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

| Tudun Biri drone strike | |
| --- | --- |
| Part of [Nigerian bandit conflict](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_bandit_conflict "Nigerian bandit conflict") | |
| Location | Tudun Biri, [Kaduna State](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaduna_State "Kaduna State"), [Nigeria](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria "Nigeria") |
| Date | 3 December 2023 |
| Attack type | Accidental drone strike |
| Deaths | 120+ (per Amnesty International Nigeria)[[1]](#cite_note-:2-1) 88+ (per Nigerian authorities)[[2]](#cite_note-:3-2) |
| Perpetrator | [Nigerian Air Force](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_Air_Force "Nigerian Air Force") |

On 3 December 2023, a [drone strike](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_strike "Drone strike") was carried out by the [Nigerian Armed Forces](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_Armed_Forces "Nigerian Armed Forces") on Tudun Biri, [Kaduna State](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaduna_State "Kaduna State"). Targeting what they thought was a group of bandits, the army mistakenly hit a village, killing at least 88 civilians.

In their campaigns against [bandits](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_bandit_conflict "Nigerian bandit conflict") and jihadist activity in northern Nigeria, drones have been heavily used by the Nigerian government.[[3]](#cite_note-3) These have led to airstrikes on civilian centers with heavy casualties, including an attack in [Nasarawa State](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasarawa_State "Nasarawa State") in January that killed 39 civilians.[[4]](#cite_note-4) A drone strike in [Kaduna State](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaduna_State "Kaduna State") in March 2023 killed three others in Sabon Gida.[[5]](#cite_note-:0-5) Survivors of the attack stated that no bandits were in Tudun Biri, and the one time there was a bandit, he was disowned.[[6]](#cite_note-:1-6)

The drone strike occurred as the villagers were celebrating [Mawlid](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mawlid "Mawlid"), the birth of the Prophet [Muhammad](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad"). A Nigerian drone flying overhead in routine counter-terrorism operations mistook the movements of the civilians for bandits, and the [Nigerian Air Force](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_Air_Force "Nigerian Air Force") called in an airstrike on the village.[[5]](#cite_note-:0-5) A survivor of the attacks stated, "I was just standing when I head loud sounds of bombs."[[6]](#cite_note-:1-6) Immediately after the attacks, the survivors fled in every direction, sleeping in the woods that night.[[6]](#cite_note-:1-6)

The Nigerian Air Force initially denied responsibility for the attacks, but later admitted that 85 people were killed.[[5]](#cite_note-:0-5) This number was stated by Kaduna State governor [Uba Sani](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uba_Sani "Uba Sani") and the Nigerian [National Emergency Management Agency](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Emergency_Management_Agency_(Nigeria) "National Emergency Management Agency (Nigeria)").[[1]](#cite_note-:2-1)[[2]](#cite_note-:3-2) [Amnesty International](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty_International "Amnesty International")'s Nigeria office, citing locals, stated that 120 people were killed in the attack.[[1]](#cite_note-:2-1) Most of the dead were children.[[1]](#cite_note-:2-1)

Fifty bodies were buried on the first day, and the remaining bodies were buried in a mass burial on December 5.[[6]](#cite_note-:1-6)
In May 2024 it was announced that two military officers would face court martial as a result of the investigation into this incident.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

President [Bola Tinubu](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bola_Tinubu "Bola Tinubu") expressed his condolences for the victims, and ordered an investigation into the airstrike.[[8]](#cite_note-8) Nigerian Army chief of staff [Taoreed Lagbaja](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taoreed_Lagbaja "Taoreed Lagbaja") attended the funeral and echoed Tinubu's sentiments.[[6]](#cite_note-:1-6)

Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Mangu_violence:
From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

| 2023 Mangu violence | |
| --- | --- |
| Part of [Herder-farmer conflicts in Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herder-farmer_conflicts_in_Nigeria "Herder-farmer conflicts in Nigeria") | |
| Location | [Mangu LGA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mangu,_Nigeria "Mangu, Nigeria"), [Plateau State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plateau_State "Plateau State"), [Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria "Nigeria") |
| Date | May 15-16, 2023 |
| Deaths | 200+ civilians killed (per local activists) 130+ civilians killed (per government officials and [Christian Association of Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Association_of_Nigeria "Christian Association of Nigeria")) |
| Perpetrator | Fulani herdsmen |

From 15 to 16 May 2023 over one hundred people were killed in an attack by Fulani herders against villagers in [Mangu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mangu,_Nigeria "Mangu, Nigeria") [Local Government Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_government_areas_of_Nigeria "Local government areas of Nigeria") of [Plateau State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plateau_State "Plateau State"), [Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria "Nigeria").

Fighting between (mostly Christian) farmers and [Fulani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulani "Fulani") herders in Central and North-West Nigeria over access to resources has been going on for several decades. Most of the violence takes place in the form of attacks on villages by Fulani herders, sometimes as reprisals for attacks by anti-Fulani vigilantes. The government response to the conflict has been largely inefficient and few arrests have been made. In recent years the security crisis has grown worse as the death toll increases and violence becomes more common.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) Prior to the conflict a farmer had let his cattle destroy a Fulani man's banana plantation which locals claimed was the trigger for the attack.[[3]](#cite_note-:0-3)

The conflict started at 2:00 AM local time on 15 May 2023, when huge numbers of Fulani gunmen attacked and burned multiple villages, including Kubwat and Fungzai where 28 and 9 people were reportedly killed, respectively.[[4]](#cite_note-:1-4) Women and children were said to be among the dead. Houses and crops were set ablaze as assailants attacked villagers using guns and machetes.[[3]](#cite_note-:0-3)[[5]](#cite_note-5)

The [Governor of Plateau State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Plateau_State "Governor of Plateau State"), [Simon Lalong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Lalong "Simon Lalong"), condemned the massacre and promised to arrest the perpetrators. The local government declared a 24-hour curfew,[[4]](#cite_note-:1-4) but locals criticized the curfew as ineffective.[[6]](#cite_note-6) On 18 May local authorities told the [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press") at least 80 people had died, and that they had arrested at least 7 suspects.[[3]](#cite_note-:0-3)[[7]](#cite_note-7)

On 17 May, [House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Representatives_(Nigeria) "House of Representatives (Nigeria)") member for Mangu LGA [Solomon Maren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solomon_Maren "Solomon Maren") said that "over 100 persons, most of them women and children" had died over the past two days and that widespread destruction of homes and crops had occurred. Maren criticized the [Buhari administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buhari_Administration "Buhari Administration") for failing to prevent such attacks.[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9)

On 22 May, the [Christian Association of Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Association_of_Nigeria "Christian Association of Nigeria") said that over the past week "about 130 people were killed, about 1,000 buildings burnt, and about 22 villages affected." Archbishop and president of the CAN [Daniel Okoh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Okoh "Daniel Okoh") deplored the massacre and called for an end to the violence.[[10]](#cite_note-:2-10) Activist Joseph Gwankat, head of the Mwaghavul Development Association, estimated the death toll to be more than 200, adding that 20,000 people are believed to have been displaced. The fighting also cut off access to certain villages.[[11]](#cite_note-11) Gwankat said that at least 125 bodies had been buried.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

On 21 May, Fulani militias passed by the town of Daika in Panyam District on motorcycles. The militants opened fire on a group of young men, killing four.[[10]](#cite_note-:2-10)

On 25 May, church leaders led a group of around 250 protesters in [Jos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos "Jos"), urging the government to take action.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

| 2023 Plateau State massacres | |

| Perpetrators | Believed to have been [Fulani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulani "Fulani") militia |
| Motive | Ethnic and religious tensions, land disputes, [herder–farmer conflicts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herder%E2%80%93farmer_conflicts_in_Nigeria "Herder–farmer conflicts in Nigeria") |
| Inquiries | [Amnesty International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty_International "Amnesty International") called for an independent investigation |
| Attacks followed previous incidents in October and November 2023 | |

A series of armed attacks occurred between 23 and 25 December 2023 in [Plateau State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plateau_State "Plateau State") in central Nigeria. They affected at least 17 rural communities in the [Nigerian local government areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_local_government_areas "Nigerian local government areas") of [Bokkos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bokkos "Bokkos") and [Barkin Ladi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barkin_Ladi "Barkin Ladi"), resulting in at least 200 deaths and injuries to more than 500 people[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) as well as significant property damage.[[3]](#cite_note-Asadu_2023-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4) Although no group claimed responsibility for the attacks, they are believed to have been committed by [Fulani militias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulani_extremism "Fulani extremism").[[3]](#cite_note-Asadu_2023-3)

[Plateau State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plateau_State "Plateau State") is in Nigeria's [Middle Belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Belt "Middle Belt") and has a history of ethnic and religious conflicts, mainly between Muslim [Fulani herders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulani_herders "Fulani herders") and Christian farmers.[[5]](#cite_note-Eboh_&_Ibrahim_2023-5) The bandit conflict began in 2011 as a result of disagreements over [land ownership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_ownership "Land ownership") and [grazing rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grazing_rights "Grazing rights") between the herders and farmers.[[6]](#cite_note-6) Banditry and insecurity are exacerbated by Nigeria's high [fertility rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fertility_rate "Fertility rate") (5.3 as of 2023), with the large youth population suffering from unemployment and [underemployment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underemployment "Underemployment") that makes them susceptible to radicalism and banditry.[[7]](#cite_note-7) [Climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change") and the expansion of agriculture also lead to increased conflict.[[8]](#cite_note-8) Previous attacks occurred in the region in April 2022 and May 2023.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

[Miyetti Allah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miyetti_Allah "Miyetti Allah") (MACBAN), an advocacy group for [Fulani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulani "Fulani") interests, accused state security personnel of colluding with farmers to attack Fulani herders. Muhammed Nuru Abdullahi, the state chairman of the MACBAN, claimed the violence began with a failed act of "[cattle rustling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cattle_rustling "Cattle rustling")" against Fulani on 23 December, where three cattle breeders were killed and the theft of 181 cows was attempted, and that 130 houses were burned in several Fulani villages on 24 December. He recommended that "in order to end the incessant clashes between farmers and herders, the Federal Government should establish [ranches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranch "Ranch") in Plateau State and other states of the Federation for [animal husbandry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_husbandry "Animal husbandry")."[[10]](#cite_note-10)

At least 17 rural communities in the regions of [Bokkos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bokkos "Bokkos") and [Barkin Ladi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barkin_Ladi "Barkin Ladi") were attacked on 23 and 24 December, leaving at least 200 people dead and over 500 wounded.[[11]](#cite_note-11) The attackers, who used guns and machetes, burned houses and other property.[[5]](#cite_note-Eboh_&_Ibrahim_2023-5)[[12]](#cite_note-

Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Yobe_State_attacks:
From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

| 2023 Yobe State attacks | |
| --- | --- |
| Part of the [Boko Haram insurgency](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boko_Haram_insurgency "Boko Haram insurgency") | |
| Location | Gurokayeya, Yobe State, Nigeria |
| Date | 30–31 October 2023 |
| Deaths | 37 |
| Injured | 7 |
| Perpetrators | [Boko Haram](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boko_Haram "Boko Haram") |

In late October 2023, two terrorist attacks perpetrated by [Boko Haram](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boko_Haram "Boko Haram") occurred in [Yobe State](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yobe_State "Yobe State"), [Nigeria](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria "Nigeria") a day apart, killing at least 37 people and injuring 7.

On 30 October, militants raided the [Gurokayeya](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurokayeya,_Nigeria?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gurokayeya, Nigeria (page does not exist)") village on motorbikes at around 19:30 [GMT](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich_Mean_Time "Greenwich Mean Time") and shot at villagers sporadically, killing at least 17.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) A resident of the village and an anti-jihadist militia stated that the attack occurred when villagers refused to pay an illicit tax to the terrorists. The shooting was the first deadly attack in Yobe State in over a year.[[3]](#cite_note-france24-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)

On 31 October, a day after the shooting in Gurokayeya, at least 20 mourners were killed when their vehicle drove over a landmine.[[5]](#cite_note-barrons-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6) The victims were returning from the burial services of the people killed in the previous attack.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The vehicle that was attacked carried 22 men from the neighboring [Karabiri](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karabiri,_Nigeria?action=edit&redlink=1 "Karabiri, Nigeria (page does not exist)") village. A member of an anti-jihadist militia stated that, “There were fears the terrorists could return and disrupt the funeral, but the people insisted on burying the dead.”[[5]](#cite_note-barrons-5)

The first attack killed at least 17 people and wounded five others, according to [Gremah Bukar](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gremah_Bukar?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gremah Bukar (page does not exist)"), a member of an anti-jihadist militia.[[3]](#cite_note-france24-3) The second attack killed 20 people and severely injured two others. Ten people died immediately while another ten died at a health center after they were rushed to it to be treated.[[8]](#cite_note-bbc.com-8) The injuries of the two survivors were so severe that the hospital they were being treated in was making arrangements to transfer them to [Yobe State Specialist Hospital Damaturu](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yobe_State_Specialist_Hospital_Damaturu?action=edit&redlink=1 "Yobe State Specialist Hospital Damaturu (page does not exist)").[[3]](#cite_note-france24-3)

The Yobe State government summoned an emergency security meeting over the attacks. In it, they blamed extremists who entered the state from the neighboring Borno State and started to study reports on the infiltration in order to prevent future attacks. Security agencies also deployed men to the site of the attacks, according to a Yobe State government security aide.[[3]](#cite_note-france24-3)

A resident of the village described the attack as one of Boko Haram's most horrific in recent times, stating that, “For a burial group to be attacked shortly after the loss of their loved ones is beyond horrific.”[[8]](#cite_note-bbc.com-8)

The President of the General Assembly is from [Latin American and Caribbean Group](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_American_and_Caribbean_Group "Latin American and Caribbean Group").

The Nigerian authorities have provided little information and no justice for a military airstrike on January 24, 2023, that killed 39 civilians and injured at least 6 others.

* The military’s unacceptable delay in owning up to the killing and injuring dozens of civilians only compounds the tragedy of this attack.
* The Nigerian military should provide full accountability for their actions and financial compensation and livelihood assistance based on the needs of the victims and their families.

(Abuja) – The [Nigerian](https://www.hrw.org/africa/nigeria) authorities have provided little information and no justice for a military airstrike on January 24, 2023 that killed 39 civilians and injured at least 6 others, Human Rights Watch said today. The government should ensure an urgent, independent, impartial, and transparent inquiry into the attack that took place in Kwatiri, a small settlement in Nasarawa State.

Almost six months after the incident, the Nigerian air force admitted for the first time, in [response](https://www.hrw.org/sites/default/files/media_2023/06/Nigerian%20air%20force%20response.pdf) to an [inquiry](https://www.hrw.org/sites/default/files/media_2023/06/HRW%20Inquiry%20to%20Nigerian%20air%20force.pdf) from Human Rights Watch, to carrying out the airstrike. It said it was an air component of Operation Whirl Stroke, a joint military, police, and department of state security operation deployed in response to security problems in and around Nasarawa State. The air force claimed it carried out the airstrike in response to “suspected terrorist” activities but provided no details.

“The military’s unacceptable delay in owning up to the killing and injuring dozens of civilians only compounds the tragedy of this shocking attack,” said [Anietie Ewang](https://www.hrw.org/about/people/anietie-ewang), Africa researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The Nigerian military should provide full accountability for their actions as well as financial compensation and livelihood assistance commensurate with the needs of the victims and their families.”

Since 2017, [over 300 people are reported to have been killed by airstrikes](https://www.sbmintel.com/2023/02/chart-of-the-week-nigeria-air-force-mishaps/) that the Nigerian air force claimed were intended for bandits or members of the Islamist armed group Boko Haram, but instead hit civilians.

On January 25, Nasarawa State Governor Abdullahi Sule [told](https://www.thecable.ng/nasarawa-explosion-drone-dropped-the-bomb-not-naf-aircraft-says-abdullahi-sule) Nigerian media that the airstrike, which hit a group of cattle herders in the settlement in Doma Local Government Area of the state, had been carried out by an unidentified drone.

Between March 13 and 15, Human Rights Watch interviewed 12 people, including two survivors of the airstrike and seven family members of victims who were killed. Human Rights Watch also reviewed and verified eight photographs showing some of the bodies and on March 14 visited a mass grave where 31 bodies were buried.

The photos showed about 17 bodies with deep perforating injuries and ghastly wounds. Human Rights Watch investigations, including interviews with victims who survived and family members of some of the deceased, revealed they were cattle herders and found no evidence that the targets of the airstrike had any link to bandit gangs or other armed groups.

On May 3, Human Rights Watch wrote to the Nigerian chief of air staff, who oversees the air force, which carries out military air operations, and the chief of defense staff, who oversees all military units including the air force, to provide details of its findings and to request answers to specific questions about the airstrike.

In a response on May 17, Air Commodore D. D. Pwajok, on behalf of the chief of air staff, acknowledged that the air force carried out the strike based “on credible intelligence and in synergy with other security forces and agencies in Nasarawa State.” The letter said that air force surveillance footage showed the movement of “suspected terrorists” who converged around “a truck suspected to be a logistics vehicle,” which arrived at the location at night and was determined to be a target for the airstrike.

The letter did not respond to key questions, including how information regarding the suspected threat was considered and verified, whether efforts were made to investigate and verify the identity of those targeted, or if any assessment was carried out before the airstrike to avoid or mitigate civilian harm. The absence of details raises the question of whether the air force carried out the airstrike based on mere suspicion. The letter concluded that the Nigerian air force is committed to upholding human rights and is open to further deliberations on the issue.

**RECENT school attacks in Borno and Oyo states have left Nigerians grappling with the troubling pattern and spread of insecurity in the country.**

In Borno state, gunmen stormed Government Day Junior Secondary School in Askira-Uba Local Government Area, abducting dozens of pupils on May 15, 2026. On the same day, three schools in Orire LGA, of Oyo State were attacked with dozens of pupils and teachers abducted, spreading fear to the South-West.

These incidents revive memories of past mass abductions such as the Chibok and Dapchi kidnappings in the North East that plunged Nigeria’s security challenges into global consciousness and drew international outrage.

Occurring a few days before the National Day of Mourning and Remembrance, these incidents highlight a surge in mass atrocities committed against Nigerians. Data mined by the ICIR, reveal that these atrocities have persisted for six years, shrinking safety in communities, markets, schools and other public spaces.

### **32,667 killed, 23,187 kidnapped in six years**

According to figures obtained from [Mass Atrocities Tracker](https://massatrocities.org/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), no fewer than 32,667 people were killed across Nigeria between 2021 and 2026. This translates to an average of about 15 deaths per day over the six-year period. 

The figures, compiled from incidents linked to insurgency, banditry, activities of the Indigenous People of Biafra (IPOB) and communal violence, show the spread in killings and abductions across different parts of the country despite repeated military operations and government assurances.

Based on the data, 6,895 were killed in 2021, at a time when several communities in Zamfara and Kaduna faced repeated mass raids by armed groups, with entire villages ransacked and residents either killed or forced to flee.

In 2022, about 5,792 deaths were recorded. The ICIR gathered that during this period, bandit attacks and communal clashes intensified across parts of the North-West and North-Central, with communities in Plateau and Benue continuing to report killings in farming settlements.

Further breakdown of the data shows that at least 4,416 people were killed in 2023 while, in 2024, deaths rose again to 5,353, with renewed attacks in Borno and continued violence in the North-West. School attacks, village raids and highway ambushes again became more frequent.

In 2025, at least 6,518 people were killed. The year saw renewed insurgent attacks in the North-East and sustained bandit violence in Zamfara, where entire communities were again forced to abandon their homes after repeated assaults. The latest data shows that between January-April, 2026, at least 3,693 people have been killed.

### **Top 5 states with highest killings**

Further breakdown shows that Borno recorded the highest number of deaths with 5,706 victims between 2021 and 2026. This is followed by Zamfara which recorded 4,396 deaths within the same period. Benue recorded 2,948 deaths making it the third most hit state. It was closely followed by Kaduna which 2,851 deaths and Plateau with 2,471 deaths within the period under review.

Other states in the ranking include Katsina with 2,144 deaths, Niger with 2,135 deaths and Sokoto with 903 killed.  Tarawa recorded 823, and Kebbi, 800 killed in the last six years.

### **Why Borno leads as epicentre of killings**

In Borno, the state’s long-running insurgency crisis has made it the main theatre of operations for Boko Haram and its breakaway faction, ISWAP (Islamic State West Africa Province). Boko Haram emerged around 2009 as an armed Islamist insurgent group in north-eastern Nigeria, launching attacks on police stations, military bases, schools, places of worship and civilian communities. The group’s campaign of violence escalated sharply after 2011, leading to mass displacement and the destruction of entire towns.

In 2016, the group split, leading to the emergence of ISWAP, which aligned itself with the Islamic State network. Since then, both groups have operated in different parts of the Lake Chad basin, with ISWAP becoming more dominant in some areas due to its more structured operations and control over territories around the Lake Chad axis.

Over the years, both groups have carried out repeated raids on rural communities, often targeting farming villages, highways, military outposts and internally displaced persons’ routes. These attacks have forced many residents in Borno to flee their homes, with thousands still living in camps or host communities years after displacement.

Asiwaju **Bola Ahmed Adekunle Tinubu** [GCFR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Commander_of_the_Order_of_the_Federal_Republic "Grand Commander of the Order of the Federal Republic") (born 29 March 1952) is a Nigerian politician serving as the 16th and current [president of Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Nigeria "President of Nigeria") since 2023.[[1]](#cite_note-1) He previously served as the [governor of Lagos State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Lagos_State "Governor of Lagos State") from 1999 to 2007 and [senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Nigeria "Senate of Nigeria") for [Lagos West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagos_West_senatorial_district "Lagos West senatorial district") in the [Third Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Nigerian_Republic "Third Nigerian Republic").[[2]](#cite_note-2)

Tinubu spent his early life in [southwestern Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_West_(Nigeria) "South West (Niger

worn in as President of Nigeria by the Chief Justice [Olukayode Ariwoola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olukayode_Ariwoola "Olukayode Ariwoola") at 10:41 AM ([WAT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Africa_Time "West Africa Time")) at an [inauguration ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inauguration_of_Bola_Tinubu "Inauguration of Bola Tinubu") held in [Eagle Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eagle_Square,_Abuja "Eagle Square, Abuja") in [Abuja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abuja "Abuja").[[83]](#cite_note-83) His government, having cleared the legal hurdles of the opposition following the [March election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Nigerian_presidential_election "2023 Nigerian presidential election"), is generally accepted unopposed and has international legitimacy.[[84]](#cite_note-84) Several heads of state and government attended the swearing-in ceremony.[[85]](#cite_note-85) Tinubu was conferred with the highest national honour of the [Grand Commander of the Order of the Federal Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Commander_of_the_Order_of_the_Federal_Republic "Grand Commander of the Order of the Federal Republic") by his predecessor [Muhammadu Buhari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammadu_Buhari "Muhammadu Buhari"), and Vice President [Kashim Shettima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashim_Shettima "Kashim Shettima") with the second highest honour of the [Grand Commander of the Order of the Niger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Commander_of_the_Order_of_the_Niger "Grand Commander of the Order of the Niger") on 25 May 2023.[[86]](#cite_note-86)

### Economic reforms

Tinubu in his inaugural address promulgated the removal of the government subsidy on fuel.[[87]](#cite_note-87) The statement in his inaugural address caused initial panic buying and an overnight increase in prices at fuel pump stations in Nigeria.[[88]](#cite_note-88) The national labour union [NLC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria_Labour_Congress "Nigeria Labour Congress") called for nationwide strike and protests over the increase in fuel price, which was later called off amidst ongoing negotiations with government representatives.[[89]](#cite_note-89) The government subsidy on fuel consumption has caused a haemorrhage on the Nigerian public purse for decades and the removal was lauded as a positive development by the [World Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Bank "World Bank") for the Nigerian economy.[[90]](#cite_note-90) On 29 May 2023, Tinubu ended the costly subsidy of fuel that had previously existed in Nigeria, bringing [privatization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privatization "Privatization") to the [petroleum industry of Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroleum_industry_in_Nigeria "Petroleum industry in Nigeria"). The subsidy had cost the Nigerian government $10 billion per year at the time it was finally ended by Tinubu.[[91]](#cite_note-:02-91)

President Tinubu on the night of 9 June suspended [Godwin Emefiele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Godwin_Emefiele "Godwin Emefiele"), the powerful [governor of the central bank of Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_the_Central_Bank_of_Nigeria "Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria").[[92]](#cite_note-92) Emefiele's suspension was the second ever a head of the apex bank in its history was removed by a Nigerian president.[[93]](#cite_note-93) Emefiele was arrested by Nigerian secret police [SSS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Security_Service_(Nigeria) "State Security Service (Nigeria)") in Lagos attempting to flee the country to Benin.[[94]](#cite_note-94) The suspension was viewed as a positive development.[[95]](#cite_note-95)[[96]](#cite_note-qz.com-96) Emefiele as a conservative banker ascribed to the old school of propping up the [Nigerian naira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_naira "Nigerian naira").[[97]](#cite_note-97)[[96]](#cite_note-qz.com-96)[[98]](#cite_note-Adeoye-98) Emefiele was replaced by one of his more economical liberal deputies Folashodun Adebisi as acting governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria in a statement by the presidency "sequel to the ongoing investigation of his office and the planned reforms in the financial sector of the economy".[[98]](#cite_note-Adeoye-98) The suspension and subsequent arrest of Emefiele by secret police on charges of terrorism financing is seen as not far removed from his ideological leanings and politicising of the apex bank with his initiatives in office such as arbitrage under the Buhari administration and a currency redesign of the Nigerian naira.[[99]](#cite_note-99) However, some observers have noted the role of politics in Emefiele's suspension amid a clandestine raise in government debt borrowing ceiling from 5% to 15% through [ways and means](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ways_and_means_committee "Ways and means committee") on the eve of the inauguration of President Tinubu.[[100]](#cite_note-100)

On the back of his suspension, the apex bank five days later on 14 June removed all foreign exchange trading restrictions and allowed the national currency to fall to its lowest ever on the market.[[101]](#cite_note-101) The move, though not unprecedented, signalled what was expected after the suspension.[[102]](#cite_note-102) Tinubu's financial reforms has been seen as surpassing the [1986 SAP regime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibrahim_Babangida "Ibrahim Babangida") in a bid to drastically overhaul the Nigerian economy and government finances since the return of democracy two decades prior.[[103]](#cite_note-103)[[104]](#cite_note-104) On 15 June, President Tinubu inaugurated the national economic council chaired by Vice President Shettima.[[105]](#cite_note-105) The Council is mandated to advise the President on economic affairs and is composed of the governor of the central bank and all state governors of the federation.[[106]](#cite_note-106) Tinubu's close associate, investment banker [Wale Edun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wale_Edun "Wale Edun"), is the monetary policy czar.[[107]](#cite_note-107)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Prime_Minister_Narendra_Modi_in_a_bilateral_meeting_with_the_President_of_Nigeria%2C_Mr._Bola_Ahmed_Tinubu%2C_in_New_Delhi_on_September_10%2C_2023.jpg/250px-Prime_Minister_Narendra_Modi_in_a_bilateral_meeting_with_the_President_of_Nigeria%2C_Mr._Bola_Ahmed_Tinubu%2C_in_New_Delhi_on_September_10%2C_2023.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Prime_Minister_Narendra_Modi_in_a_bilateral_meeting_with_the_President_of_Nigeria,_Mr._Bola_Ahmed_Tinubu,_in_New_Delhi_on_September_10,_2023.jpg)

Indian Prime Minister [Narendra Modi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narendra_Modi "Narendra Modi") meeting with Tinubu at the [2023 G20 New Delhi summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_G20_New_Delhi_summit "2023 G20 New Delhi summit")

### Cabinet and appointments

President Tinubu appointed on 3 June Senator [George Akume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Akume "George Akume") as the [Secretary to the Government of the Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_to_the_Government_of_the_Federation "Secretary to the Government of the Federation") and [Femi Gbajabiamila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Femi_Gbajabiamila "Femi Gbajabiamila") as [Chief of Staff to the President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_of_Staff_to_the_President_(Nigeria) "Chief of Staff to the President (Nigeria)").[[108]](#cite_note-108) Tinubu suspended the [EFCC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_and_Financial_Crimes_Commission "Economic and Financial Crimes Commission") chairman [Abdulrasheed Bawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdulrasheed_Bawa "Abdulrasheed Bawa") on 9 June and Nigerian secret police arrested him for abuse of office on the same day following a standoff between SSS agents and the EFCC in Lagos.[[109]](#cite_note-109)[[110]](#cite_note-110) His suspension like Emefiele's involved a lot of intrigues as Bawa had previously placed Tinubu under investigation.[[111]](#cite_note-111) Bawa was replaced with Abdulkarim Chukkol as acting chairman of the EFCC.[[112]](#cite_note-112)

President Tinubu on 19 June proclaimed Mallam [Nuhu Ribadu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuhu_Ribadu "Nuhu Ribadu") as the [National Security Adviser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Security_Adviser_(Nigeria) "National Security Adviser (Nigeria)").[[113]](#cite_note-113) The appointment of Nuhu Ribadu, a former police officer, was viewed as a radical turn from the military establishment which has long dominated the state security apparatus of Nigeria.[[114]](#cite_note-114) President Tinubu purged the leadership of the entire armed and paramilitary forces on 19 June retiring in the process over one hundred and fifty [major generals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major-general_(Nigeria) "Major-general (Nigeria)").[[115]](#cite_note-115)[[116]](#cite_note-116) The direction of state security under Tinubu is expected to be led by civilian control of the military under the Office of the National Security Adviser, a statutory constitutional body established in 1993.[[117]](#cite_note-117)

calls for a coalition government in order to bring opposition leaders under him.[[119]](#cite_note-119) A constitutional amendment passed by his predecessor made provisions for the President to appoint Ministers within the first sixty days in office. Tinubu dissolved the boards of all ministries, departments and agencies of Nigeria on 19 June.[[120]](#cite_note-120) Having spent one month in office and with the conclusion of parliamentary leadership elections Tinubu is constrained by law to send ministerial nominations to the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Nigeria "Senate of Nigeria") for hearing before July 29.[[121]](#cite_note-121)

On 16 February 2024, Tinubu appointed [Oyetunde Oladimeji Ojo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oyetunde_Oladimeji_Ojo?action=edit&redlink=1 "Oyetunde Oladimeji Ojo (page does not exist)"), who is married to his daughter [Folashade Tinubu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folashade_Tinubu?action=edit&redlink=1 "Folashade Tinubu (page does not exist)"), as head of the [Federal Housing Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Housing_Authority "Federal Housing Authority"), producing criticism for its alleged nepotism.[[122]](#cite_note-122)

### Culture

On 29 May 2024, Tinubu signed into law an act readopting *[Nigeria, We Hail Thee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria,_We_Hail_Thee "Nigeria, We Hail Thee")*, which was the country's [national anthem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_anthem "National anthem") from 1960 to 1978, as its national anthem, replacing *[Arise, O Compatriots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arise,_O_Compatriots "Arise, O Compatriots")*.[[123]](#cite_note-:0-123) Tinubu declared a state of emergency in Rivers State removing the governor and replacing him with an appointed administrator.[[123]](#cite_note-:0-123) The moved was widely criticized as being grotesquely unconstitutional.[[123]](#cite_note-:0-123)

### Coup plot

In late September 2025, a coup plot against the Tinubu administration which was uncovered by Nigerian military intelligence and leaked by Sahara Reporters.[[124]](#cite_note-124)[[125]](#cite_note-125) [Independence Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence_Day_(Nigeria) "Independence Day (Nigeria)") military parade scheduled for 1 October 2025[[126]](#cite_note-126) was cancelled,[[127]](#cite_note-127) sixteen military officers were arrested by the [Defence Intelligence Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defence_Intelligence_Agency_(Nigeria) "Defence Intelligence Agency (Nigeria)") including a brigadier general, colonel, four lieutenant colonels, five majors, two captains, a naval lieutenant commander and an air force squadron leader.[[128]](#cite_note-128) Initial reports of the plot were denied by the military who downplayed the arrests as disciplinary in nature.[[129]](#cite_note-129)[[130]](#cite_note-130) The plot allegedly involved officers of northerner extraction masterminded by Colonel Mohammed Ma'aji,[[131]](#cite_note-131) and included an officer attached to the office of the national security adviser with alleged financial support from former governor and petroleum minister [Timipre Slyva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timipre_Sylva "Timipre Sylva").[[132]](#cite_note-132)[[133]](#cite_note-133)[[134]](#cite_note-134) The plotters planned to violently overthrow the federal government on 25 October by assassinating the President and several [high-ranking government officials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_presidential_line_of_succession "Nigerian presidential line of succession").[[135]](#cite_note-135) Tinubu replaced the military service chiefs on 18 October, with General [Olufemi Oluyede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olufemi_Oluyede "Olufemi Oluyede") promoted to [chief of defence staff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_of_Defence_Staff_(Nigeria) "Chief of Defence Staff (Nigeria)") and investigations are still ongoing.[[136]](#cite_note-136)

### Civil conflict

#### US strikes

In early November 2025, U.S. President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") ordered the United States military to prepare for [military action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_military_interventions "United States military interventions") in Nigeria. Trump cited the alleged [violent killings of Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Christians_in_Nigeria "Persecution of Christians in Nigeria") and alleged violations of religious freedom as the reason for designating Nigeria as a “[country of particular concern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_of_Particular_Concern "Country of Particular Concern")” for failure to address violent [communal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communal_conflicts_in_Nigeria "Communal conflicts in Nigeria") and [religious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_violence_in_Nigeria "Religious violence in Nigeria") conflicts in the country by [Islamist insurgents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamist_insurgency_in_Nigeria "Islamist insurgency in Nigeria"), [bandits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_bandit_conflict "Nigerian bandit conflict"), [extremists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulani_extremism_in_Nigeria "Fulani extremism in Nigeria") and [herder-farmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herder%E2%80%93farmer_conflicts_in_Nigeria "Herder–farmer conflicts in Nigeria") clashes.[[137]](#cite_note-137)[[138]](#cite_note-138)[[139]](#cite_note-139)[[140]](#cite_note-140) President Tinubu rejected Trump's accusation and spoke of the Nigerian government's efforts to protect its citizens regardless of religion.[[141]](#cite_note-141)

On 25 December 2025, at the request of Tinubu's administration the United States carried out a strike against the [Islamic State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_State_%E2%80%93_West_Africa_Province "Islamic State – West Africa Province") in [northwest Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_West_(Nigeria) "North West (Nigeria)"). U.S. President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), claimed the U.S. struck in order to protect Christians from perceived [religious violence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_violence_in_Nigeria "Religious violence in Nigeria") in northern Nigeria, the U.S. strike is the first foreign military intervention in post-independence Nigeria.[[142]](#cite_note-142)

### Foreign policy

Tinubu embarked on his first foreign visit as Nigerian president to Paris on 21 June to attend a global financial summit held at [Palais Brongniart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_Brongniart "Palais Brongniart") from 22 to 24 June.[[143]](#cite_note-143) He left Paris for London on a "private visit" where he met with his predecessor Muhammadu Buhari.[[144]](#cite_note-144)

In August 2023, he advocated for military intervention into [Niger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niger "Niger") during the [2023 Nigerien crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Nigerien_crisis "2023 Nigerien crisis").[[145]](#cite_note-145) This was criticised by the opposition.[[146]](#cite_note-146)

In December 2025, Tinubu authorized the [Nigerian Armed Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_Armed_Forces "Nigerian Armed Forces") to carry out a military intervention in neighbouring Benin to support the country's government following a [coup attempt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Beninese_coup_attempt "2025 Beninese coup attempt") against President [Patrice Talon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrice_Talon "Patrice Talon").[[147]](#cite_note-147)

In May 2026, Tinubu embarked on a three-day visit to France to meet with global investors in defense of his economic reforms.[[148]](#cite_note-148)

## Ideology and public image

Tinubu has throughout his political career espoused a comprehensive political and economic platform. Tinubu's ideal of [progressivism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressivism "Progressivism") include the values of [egalitarianism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egalitarianism "Egalitarianism"), [social justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_justice "Social justice"), [liberty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty "Liberty"), and the recognition of [fundamental rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_rights "Fundamental rights"). He views the state as a positive advocate for the [public welfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_welfare "Public welfare") and its intervention in Nigerian society as necessary to ensure equality, justice, and social harmony.[[149]](#cite_note-149) This ideal is not so far removed from his activism of democracy during the [military dictatorship in Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_dictatorship_in_Nigeria "Military dictatorship in Nigeria").[[150]](#cite_note-150)

### Economic views

His presidency and economic policies, which are known as Tinubunomics,[[151]](#cite_note-151) are expected to be a politico-ideological departure from [Buharism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buharism "Buharism"), albeit most international economists are yet to ascertain the nature of this departure in economic terms; reforms in his first month in office have shown a departure from the previous administration.[[152]](#cite_note-152)[[153]](#cite_note-153) The World Bank and [IMF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMF "IMF") have pointed out the need for the incoming government to establish macro-structural adjustments on the scale of the late 1980s reform to re-herald the Nigerian economy amidst a global slowdown.[[154]](#cite_note-154) Tinubunomics has been outlined in a book he co-authored with Brian Browne, an American consul general in Lagos.[[155]](#cite_note-155)[[156]](#cite_note-156)

### *The Lion of Bourdillon*

Tinubu has been widely perceived as the "[Godfather](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/godfatherism "wiktionary:godfatherism") of Lagos".[[157]](#cite_note-157) His role in pulling the strings of the mega city-state was exposed in *[The Lion of Bourdillon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lion_of_Bourdillon "The Lion of Bourdillon")*, a 2015 documentary film highlighting Tinubu's political and financial grip on the city-state. Tinubu filed a ₦150 billion libel suit against the producers, [Africa Independent Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa_Independent_Television "Africa Independent Television") (AIT).[[158]](#cite_note-158) The documentary ceased airing on 6 March 2015. He has attempted to strongarm the political process, including in December 2009, when it was reported that Fashola and Tinubu had fallen out over the issue of Fashola's re-election as Governor of Lagos in 2011, with Tinubu preferring the commissioner for environment, [Muiz Banire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dr._Muiz_Adeyemi_Banire "Dr. Muiz Adeyemi Banire").[[159]](#cite_note-159) A similar conflict took place in 2015 over Fashola's successor, [Akinwunmi Ambode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akinwunmi_Ambode "Akinwunmi Ambode"), pitting Fashola against Tinubu, who threw his full weight behind Ambode.[[160]](#cite_note-160) Ambode succeeded Fashola, was ousted by Tinubu and replaced by incumbent [Babajide Sanwo-Olu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babajide_Sanwo-Olu "Babajide Sanwo-Olu").[[161]](#cite_note-161)[[162]](#cite_note-162)

### Allegations of corruption

In 1993, his assets were frozen by the United States government as a result of a court case asserting that the American government had "[probable cause](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probable_cause "Probable cause")" to believe Tinubu's American bank accounts held the proceeds of [heroin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heroin "Heroin") dealing. He settled with the U.S. government and forfeited about $460,000 later that year. Court documents and later reporting on the case suggested he worked in league with two [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago") heroin dealers.[[163]](#cite_note-Bloomberg_News_Graft-163)[[164]](#cite_note-164)[[165]](#cite

On 26 July 2023, [a coup d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Nigerien_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "2023 Nigerien coup d'état") occurred in [Niger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niger "Niger"), during which the country's presidential guard removed and detained president [Mohamed Bazoum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Bazoum "Mohamed Bazoum"). Subsequently, General [Abdourahamane Tchiani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdourahamane_Tchiani "Abdourahamane Tchiani"), the Commander of the Presidential Guard, proclaimed himself the leader of the country and established the [National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Council_for_the_Safeguard_of_the_Homeland "National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland"), after confirming the success of the coup.[[5]](#cite_note-7)[[6]](#cite_note-8)[[7]](#cite_note-9)[[8]](#cite_note-ajtchiani-10)

In response to this development, the [Economic Community of West African States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECOWAS "ECOWAS") (ECOWAS) issued an ultimatum on 30 July, giving the coup leaders in Niger one week to reinstate Bazoum, with the threat of [international sanctions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_sanctions "International sanctions") and potential [use of force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Use_of_force "Use of force").[[9]](#cite_note-11)[[10]](#cite_note-12) When the deadline of the ultimatum expired on 6 August, no military intervention was initiated; however, on 10 August, ECOWAS took the step of activating its standby force.[[11]](#cite_note-NC-13)[[12]](#cite_note-BE-14)[[13]](#cite_note-DS-15)[[14]](#cite_note-EL-16) Previously in 2017, ECOWAS had launched a [military intervention to restore democracy in The Gambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECOWAS_military_intervention_in_the_Gambia "ECOWAS military intervention in the Gambia") during a [constitutional crisis within the country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016%E2%80%932017_Gambian_constitutional_crisis "2016–2017 Gambian constitutional crisis").

All active member states of ECOWAS, except for Cape Verde, pledged to engage their armed forces in the event of an ECOWAS-led military intervention against the Nigerien junta.[[15]](#cite_note-17) Conversely, the military juntas in Burkina Faso and Mali announced they would send troops in support of the junta were such a military intervention launched while [forming a mutual defense pact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_of_Sahel_States "Alliance of Sahel States").[[16]](#cite_note-18)[[17]](#cite_note-PO-19)

On 24 February 2024, ECOWAS announced that it was lifting sanctions on Niger, purportedly for [humanitarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanitarianism "Humanitarianism") purposes.[[1]](#cite_note-WA-1)

On 26 July 2023, President [Mohamed Bazoum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Bazoum "Mohamed Bazoum"), [First Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Lady_of_Niger "First Lady of Niger") [Hadiza Bazoum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadiza_Bazoum "Hadiza Bazoum"), and their son, Salem Bazoum, were detained at the [Presidential Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Palace,_Niamey "Presidential Palace, Niamey") in [Niamey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niamey "Niamey"), and Interior Minister [Hamadou Souley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamadou_Souley "Hamadou Souley") was also arrested. The coup was led by General [Abdourahamane Tchiani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdourahamane_Tchiani "Abdourahamane Tchiani"), whom Bazoum had planned to relieve from his position.[[18]](#cite_note-20)[[19]](#cite_note-21)[[20]](#cite_note-NS-22)[[21]](#cite_note-23)[[22]](#cite_note-24) In the evening, [Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Force_of_Niger "Air Force of Niger") Colonel-Major [Amadou Abdramane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amadou_Abdramane "Amadou Abdramane") announced on state television that Bazoum had been removed from power and announced the formation of a [National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Council_for_the_Safeguard_of_the_Homeland "National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland"), dissolution of the country's Constitution, the suspension of all state institutions, the closure of borders, and a nationwide curfew from 22:00 until 05:00 local time, while warning against any foreign intervention.[[20]](#cite_note-NS-22)[[23]](#cite_note-25)[[24]](#cite_note-26) Subsequently, all activities by [political parties in the country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_political_parties_in_Niger "List of political parties in Niger") were ordered suspended until further notice.[[25]](#cite_note-27)

Despite his detention, Bazoum has so far refused to resign.[[26]](#cite_note-bbc2-28) While declaring himself acting head of state and calling for resistance against the coup,[[26]](#cite_note-bbc2-28) Bazoum's Foreign Minister [Hassoumi Massaoudou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hassoumi_Massaoudou "Hassoumi Massaoudou") told [France 24](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_24 "France 24") that the country's "legal and legitimate power" remained with the President.[[27]](#cite_note-29) However, the leadership of the Nigerien armed forces declared its support for the coup to protect the President and avoid "a deadly confrontation."[[28]](#cite_note-30)

On 28 July, Tchiani proclaimed himself as the president of the junta, saying that he had deposed Bazoum to avoid "the gradual and inevitable demise" of the country and accusing him of covering up the country's situation. Tchiani did not give a timeline for a return to civilian rule.[[29]](#cite_note-f24tchiani-31)[[30]](#cite_note-32)[[8]](#cite_note-ajtchiani-10)

The [Economic Community of West African States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Community_of_West_African_States "Economic Community of West African States") (ECOWAS) is a regional, political and economic union of fifteen countries in West Africa, covering an area of 5,114,162 km2 (1,974,589 sq mi) and with an estimated population of over 387 million in 2019. Established in 1975, ECOWAS aims to achieve collective self-sufficiency for its member states by creating a single large trade bloc.[[31]](#cite_note-33)[[32]](#cite_note-34)

ECOWAS also serves as a [peacekeeping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peacekeeping "Peacekeeping") force in the region, with member states occasionally sending joint military forces to intervene in the bloc's member countries at times of political instability and unrest. In recent years these included interventions in [Sierra Leone in 1997](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Leone_Civil_War "Sierra Leone Civil War"), [Ivory Coast in 2003](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Ivorian_Civil_War "First Ivorian Civil War"), [Liberia in 1990](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Liberian_Civil_War "First Liberian Civil War") [and 2003](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Liberian_Civil_War "Second Liberian Civil War"), [Guinea-Bissau in 1999](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinea-Bissau_Civil_War "Guinea-Bissau Civil War") [and 2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Guinea-Bissau_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "2012 Guinea-Bissau coup d'état"), [Mali in 2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Mali_conflict "Northern Mali conflict"), and [the Gambia in 2017](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECOWAS_military_intervention_in_the_Gambia "ECOWAS military intervention in the Gambia").[[33]](#cite_note-35)[[34]](#cite_note-36)[[35]](#cite_note-37)

The United States, France, and many other countries and groups have been involved in [Niger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niger "Niger") because of the [Islamist insurgency in the Sahel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamist_insurgency_in_the_Sahel "Islamist insurgency in the Sahel"), which in turn triggered the [Jihadist insurgency in Niger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jihadist_insurgency_in_Niger "Jihadist insurgency in Niger") led by [Al-Qaeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Qaeda "Al-Qaeda"), the [Islamic State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_State "Islamic State") group and [Boko Haram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boko_Haram "Boko Haram").[[36]](#cite_note-38)[[37]](#cite_note-39)[[38]](#cite_note-40)[[39]](#cite_note-41) The United States, France, and [Turkey](https:

## The Human Rights System Is Under Threat: A Call to Action

![](/sites/default/files/styles/square/public/media_2023/03/202303staff_tirana_hassan.jpeg?h=39a634af&itok=TZSmfDi7)

Former Executive Director

We only have to look at the human rights challenges of 2023 to tell us what we need to do differently in 2024. It was a formidable year not only for human rights suppression and wartime atrocities but also for selective government outrage and transactional diplomacy that carried profound costs for the rights of those not in on the deal. Yet amid the gloom, we saw signs of hope showing the possibility of a different path.

 
Renewed hostilities between Israel and Hamas and in Sudan caused tremendous suffering, as did ongoing conflicts in Ukraine, Myanmar, Ethiopia, and the Sahel. Governments struggled to deal with the hottest year on record and the onslaught of wildfires, drought, and storms that wreaked havoc on millions of people in Bangladesh, Libya, and Canada. Economic inequality rose around the world, as did anger about the policy decisions that have left many people struggling to survive. The rights of women and girls and lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) people faced harsh backlashes in many places, exemplified by the Taliban’s gender persecution in Afghanistan.

 
The drivers of these human rights crises and their consequences often transcend borders and cannot be solved by governments acting alone. Understanding and responding to these threats needs to be rooted in universal principles of international human rights and the rule of law. These ideas built on shared human histories agreed upon by nations across all regions 75 years ago in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the basis for all contemporary human rights conventions and treaties.

 
This foundation is needed now more than ever. But this very system we rely on to protect the human rights of people everywhere is under threat. Every time a government overlooks or rejects these universal and globally accepted principles, someone pays a price – in freedoms and liberties, in their health or livelihood, and at times their lives.

Governments that could play a role in helping to improve human rights frequently adopt double standards in applying the human rights framework, which chips away at trust in the institutions responsible for enforcing and protecting rights. Governments that are vocal in condemning Israeli government war crimes against civilians in Gaza but silent about Chinese government crimes against humanity in Xinjiang, or demand international prosecution for Russian war crimes in Ukraine while undermining accountability for past US abuses in Afghanistan, weaken the belief in the universality of human rights and the legitimacy of the laws designed to protect them.

 
In transactional diplomacy, governments disregard the benefits of long-term relationships built on human rights principles to achieve immediate, short-term trade or security gains. When governments pick and choose which obligations to enforce, they perpetuate injustice not only in the present but in the future for those whose rights have been sacrificed – and can embolden abusive governments to extend the reach of their repression. The moral foundation of international human rights demands consistency and steadfastness.

 
Governments have found it easier to disregard human rights issues in the international arena in part because the international community is not challenging their violations of human rights at home. Across regions, autocrats have worked to erode the independence of key institutions vital for protecting human rights and shrink the space for expressions of dissent with the same end game in mind: to exercise power without constraint.

 
But just as these threats are interconnected, so too is the power of the human rights framework to deliver on the promise of protecting people’s freedom and dignity, no matter who they are or where they live. The protection of human rights has advanced on multiple fronts.

 
After three years of diplomatic negotiations and a decade of campaigning by civil society groups, 83 countries adopted a political declaration to better protect civilians from the use of explosive weapons in populated areas during armed conflict. The international pledge is the first to formally address the long-standing practice of warring parties to use aerial bombing, artillery, rockets, and missiles in villages, towns, and cities – the leading cause of civilian casualties in armed conflict around the world.

 
It goes further than simply urging better compliance with the laws of war by committing its signatories to adopt policies and practices that prevent and address harm. Six of the world’s top eight arms exporters – the United States, France, Germany, Italy, the United Kingdom, and South Korea – have adopted the declaration, as well as 25 of 31 NATO member states.

 
A number of countries addressed the rights of long-marginal
