Contents of https://aoav.org.uk/2023/kaduna-85-civilians-killed-66-injured-in-mistaken-nigerian-air-strike-during-religious-celebrations-in-tudun-biri-village-3-dec/:
Late on Sunday 3 December, villagers gathered in Tudun Biri to celebrate [Maulud](https://www.voanews.com/a/many-feared-dead-as-nigerian-military-airstrike-hits-local-village-/7384126.html), the birthday of the Prophet Muhammad. A military [drone](https://apnews.com/article/nigeria-kaduna-tudun-biri-military-drone-14a73c4d7587a2d5b6ab3cf9cf0b3bbb) on a routine counterterrorism operation mistook their movement patterns for those of bandits, and an airstrike was called in.

 85 people have been [buried](https://www.africanews.com/2023/12/06/nigeria-army-drone-strike-error-kills-85-civilians-at-muslim-festival/), while up to 66 were injured in the strike, which came in [two](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-africa-67621882) parts: the first strike hit the venue, while the second targeted people responding to the attack.

While Nigerian military leadership initially denied the air strike, they later confirmed that security forces [mistook](https://crisis24.garda.com/alerts/2023/12/nigeria-protests-possible-across-kaduna-state-over-coming-days-following-airstrike-that-killed-at-least-85-civilians-dec-3) the civilians for militants. President Bola Tinubu has ordered a thorough [investigation](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/nigerias-president-calls-investigation-after-drone-attack-kills-85-2023-12-05/) of the incident.

![](https://aoav.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/Screenshot-2023-12-06-at-14.09.57-700x394.jpg)

---

As has been widely documented, this is not the first time civilians have been killed and injured in Nigerian air strikes targeting armed groups. Since 2010, AOAV has recorded 83 airstrikes carried out by the Nigerian Air Force (NAF) in the country, 14 of which have killed 399 civilians and injured 310. Air strikes are the second most injurious explosive weapon to civilians in Nigeria after improvised explosive devices, which have caused 89% (9,649) of civilian casualties from explosive weapons in the country since 2010, across 439 incidents.

![](https://aoav.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/000-1-700x525.jpg)

---

![](https://aoav.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/001-1-700x525.jpg)

---

Borno and Kaduna are the most affected states for such attacks, with 376 civilians killed and injured in NAF air strikes in Borno, and 160 in Kaduna. Other states where civilians have been harmed in NAF strikes are Zamfara (82 civilian casualties), Adamawa (35), Yobe (32), Katsina (14), Niger (6), and Nasarawa (4).

While villages account for the majority of NAF strikes which have resulted in civilian harm, causing 242 civilian casualties across 9 incidents (168 killed, 74 injured), one strike on an IDP camp in 2017 caused 285 civilian casualties (115 killed, 170 injured). Other affected locations include public gatherings (152 civilian casualties), and agricultural lands (24).

![](https://aoav.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/003-700x525.jpg)

---

Overall, AOAV has recorded 559 incidents of explosive weapons use in Nigeria since 2010, killing 4,455 civilians and injuring 6,407. So far, 2023 is the most injurious year for civilians in Nigeria since 2018, with 60 incidents of explosive weapons use resulting in 336 reported civilian casualties.  In 2022, Nigeria witnessed the highest levels of civilian harm from explosive weapons since 2018, predominantly due the increased activity of non-state actors in Nigeria: incidents of explosive weapon use by non-state actors rose by 138% in 2022, from 13 to 31 incidents, with Boko Haram and Islamic State’s affiliate in Nigeria, Islamic State-West Africa Province (ISWAP), as the main known perpetrators. Overall, 200 civilian casualties were attributed to non-state actors last year.

![](https://aoav.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/004-700x525.jpg)

---

Possibly in response to this, state-perpetrated incidents of explosive violence also increased significantly, rising by 278% from 9 to 34, with reported civilian casualties of such attacks increasing from 58 to 96. Reflecting this status quo, IEDs caused the majority, 59% (176), of civilian casualties in 2022, while air-launched weapons caused 33% (100).

The **Nigerian Defence Academy** (**NDA**) is a military university based in [Kaduna](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaduna_(city) "Kaduna (city)"), Nigeria, that trains [officer cadets](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Officer_cadets "Officer cadets") for commissioning into one of the three services of the [Nigerian Armed Forces](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_Armed_Forces "Nigerian Armed Forces"): the [Army](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_Army "Nigerian Army"), the [Navy](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_Navy "Nigerian Navy"), and the [Air Force](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_Air_Force "Nigerian Air Force"). The duration of training at the Nigerian Defence Academy is five years (four years academic and one year military).[[1]](#cite_note-1)

The Nigerian Defence Academy (NDA) was established on 5 February 1964 as a reorganisation of the Royal Military Forces Training College (RMFTC), which had earlier been renamed the [Nigerian Military](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_Armed_Forces "Nigerian Armed Forces") Training College (NMTC) following Nigeria’s independence in 1960.[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)

At its establishment, the Nigerian Defence Academy was modelled after the Indian National Defence Academy in Khadakwasla, Pune, India. The first intake consisted of a small number of [cadets](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadets_(youth_program) "Cadets (youth program)"), and early training was conducted with assistance from officers of the [Indian Army](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Army "Indian Army"), including its first Commandant, Brigadier M. R. Varma.[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)

During the early years, the academy played a key role in the professionalisation of the [Nigerian Armed Forces](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_Armed_Forces "Nigerian Armed Forces"), particularly during the [Nigerian Civil War](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_Civil_War "Nigerian Civil War") (1967–1970), when it helped produce officers for rapid military expansion.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

By the late 1970s, the Nigerian Defence Academy had transitioned to predominantly Nigerian instructional staff, following an early period in which training was supported by officers of the Indian Army. This shift formed part of a broader process of indigenisation of military training institutions in Nigeria.[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10)

In 1985, the academy began awarding bachelor's degrees to officer cadets in addition to military training, formally integrating academic education with military instruction.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

In 2011, the academy admitted its first female cadets into the Regular Combatant Course, marking a major development in its admission policy.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

In 2021, the academy was attacked by armed gunmen, resulting in the death of officers and raising concerns about security within military institutions in Nigeria.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

## Campus and facilities

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nigerian_Defence_Academy&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Campus and facilities")]

The Nigerian Defence Academy is located in Afaka, Kaduna State. The academy occupies a large training and academic campus which includes lecture halls, laboratories, cadet hostels, parade grounds, military training fields, a central library and sports facilities.[[14]](#cite_note-14)

The academy also maintains facilities for physical combat training, weapons handling and field exercises as part of officer training.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

The current Commandant is [Major General](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_General "Major General") Oluyemi Olatoye. He took over from Major General Abdul Khalifah Ibrahim in October 2025.[[16]](#cite_note-:1-16)

**Human rights in Nigeria** are [protected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protection "Protection") under the [current constitution of 1999](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Nigeria "Constitution of Nigeria").[[1]](#cite_note-1) While [Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria "Nigeria") has made major improvements in [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights "Human rights") under this constitution, the [American Human Rights Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States'_Country_Reports_on_Human_Rights_Practices "United States' Country Reports on Human Rights Practices") of 2012 notes several areas in need of improvement, including:[[2]](#cite_note-2) abuses by [Boko Haram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boko_Haram "Boko Haram"), killings by government forces, lack of [social equality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_equality "Social equality") and issues with [freedom of speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_speech "Freedom of speech"). The [Human Rights Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_Watch "Human Rights Watch")'s 2015 World Report states that intensified violence by [Boko Haram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boko_Haram "Boko Haram"), restrictions of [LGBT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT "LGBT") rights and government corruption continue to undermine the status of [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights "Human rights") in [Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria "Nigeria").[[3]](#cite_note-:0-3)

## Fundamental Human Right of a Nigerian Constitution

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Human_rights_in_Nigeria&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Fundamental Human Right of a Nigerian Constitution")]

The constitution's chapter 4 of the Nigerian Human Rights guarantess the:[[4]](#cite_note-4)

* Right of life
* Right of dignity of human persons
* Right to person liberty.
* Right to fair hearing
* Right to private and family life
* Right of freedom of thought conscience and religion
* Right to freedom of expression and the press
* Right of peaceful assembly and association
* Right of freedom of movement
* Right to freedom from discrimination
* Right to acquire and own immovable property
* Compulsory acquisition of property
* Restriction on and derogation from fundamental human rights
* Special jurisdiction of high court and legal aid.

## History since independence

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Human_rights_in_Nigeria&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History since independence")]

In the period between [Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria "Nigeria")'s [independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence "Independence") in 1960 and return to democracy in 1999, the country had two Heads of State, one appointed, one military successor and 7 [coups d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coup_d'%C3%A9tat "Coup d'état"); i.e. government takeovers by military leaders. Architects of most of the coups sought to justify usurpation of power by alleging corruption or incapacity of the incumbent leader. In 1979, [Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria "Nigeria") adopted a [presidential system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_system "Presidential system") to institute a legal process of choosing a leader by enacting a new constitution. This constitution was also intended to guarantee [fundamental human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_human_rights "Fundamental human rights"), but has largely been ineffective.

The regime of General [Ibrahim Babangida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibrahim_Babangida "Ibrahim Babangida"), among others, was noted for egregious [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights "Human rights") abuses.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

Although Nigeria has been active in signing and ratifying [international human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Human_Rights "International Human Rights") treaties over the years, it has seen challenges when trying to implement these treaties [domestically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestic_policy "Domestic policy"). Nigeria operates under a [dualist system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monism_and_dualism_in_international_law#Dualism "Monism and dualism in international law") and cannot apply international treaties unless they are ratified by the [legislative houses in Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_(Nigeria) "National Assembly (Nigeria)"). Furthermore, although the [Nigerian constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Nigeria "Constitution of Nigeria") protects civil and political rights, international treaties like the [African Charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Charter_on_Human_and_Peoples'_Rights "African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights") are intended to expand protection to cultural, socio-economic, and group rights. **Natural disasters in Nigeria** are mainly related to the [climate of Nigeria](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_of_Nigeria "Climate of Nigeria"), which has been reported to cause loss of lives and [properties](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Property "Property").[[1]](#cite_note-1) A [natural disaster](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_disaster "Natural disaster") might be caused by [flooding](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flood "Flood"), [landslides](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landslide "Landslide"), and [insect](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insect "Insect") infestation, among others.[[2]](#cite_note-2) To be classified as a [disaster](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disaster "Disaster"), there is need to be a profound [environmental](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_environment "Natural environment") effect or human loss which must lead to financial loss.[[3]](#cite_note-3) This occurrence has become an issue of concern, threatening large [populations](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_(biology) "Population (biology)") living in diverse [environments](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_environment "Natural environment") in recent [years](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year "Year").[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)

[Nigeria](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria "Nigeria") has encountered several forms of [disaster](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disaster "Disaster"), which range from [flooding](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flood "Flood"), [soil](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soil_erosion "Soil erosion") and [coastal erosion](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coastal_erosion "Coastal erosion"), [landslides](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landslide "Landslide"), [tidal waves](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_surge "Storm surge"), [coastal erosion](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coastal_erosion "Coastal erosion"), [sand-storms](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sand_storms "Sand storms"), [oil spillage](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_spill "Oil spill"), [locust/insect](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locust_(insect) "Locust (insect)") infestations, and other [man-made disasters](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man-made_disasters "Man-made disasters").[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-google.com-8) It can be said that the country's under protected and expansive environment contributed to making the people especially [vulnerable](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulnerability "Vulnerability") to these [disasters](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disaster "Disaster"). Other dangers include northern [dust storms](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dust_storm "Dust storm"), which is usually from [northern](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Region,_Nigeria "Northern Region, Nigeria") states to southern, causing damages through large deposits of [dust](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dust "Dust") and [dirt](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirt "Dirt") from these [regions](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Region "Region"). [Hail](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hail "Hail") is another cause, which rarely occurs in parts of Nigeria, leading to [damage](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damage "Damage") of [crops](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crop "Crop") and properties.[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10)

### Drought and desertification

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Natural_disasters_in_Nigeria&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Drought and desertification")]

Drought stands as a significant contributor to [desertification](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desertification "Desertification"). The absence of a universally accepted, precise, and objective definition for drought has posed a substantial challenge in studying this phenomenon. It's crucial to recognize that differing definitions can yield distinct conclusions concerning drought. For instance, if the definition relies on rainfall levels, it's conceivable that when summarizing rainfall statistics over a calendar year, no drought may be apparent, even though moisture supply during the growing season may indicate otherwise. In the context of food security, drought can be defined as a naturally occurring phenomenon, often exacerbated by human activities, which persists over a specific period in a particular region, leading to a substantial drop in precipitation levels, resulting in land degradation and significantly reduced agricultural yields. However, it's important to emphasize that due to drought's multifaceted impact on various societal sectors, the need for multiple definitions exists.[[11]](#cite_note-11) Factors such as the specific problem being investigated, data availability, and climatic and regional characteristics play a role in determining the appropriate definition for an event.[[12]](#cite_note-12) Natural disasters like floods and droughts have a devastating effect on food production, storage, nutrition, and quality in countries with poor incomes.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

**Maiduguri**[Listen](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/7/75/Maiduguri_01.ogg/Maiduguri_01.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](/wiki/File:Maiduguri_01.ogg "File:Maiduguri 01.ogg") ( [*my-DOO-guurr-ee*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")) is the capital and the largest city of [Borno State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borno_State "Borno State") in north-eastern [Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria "Nigeria"), on the continent of Africa. The city sits along the seasonal [Ngadda River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ngadda_River "Ngadda River") which disappears into the *Firki* swamps in the areas around [Lake Chad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Chad "Lake Chad").[[3]](#cite_note-britannica-3) Maiduguri was founded in 1907 as a [military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military "Military") outpost by the [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland "United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland") during the [colonial period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonial_Nigeria "Colonial Nigeria"). As of 2022, Maiduguri is estimated to have a population of approximately two million people, in the metropolitan area.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Rabih_statue.jpg/250px-Rabih_statue.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rabih_statue.jpg)

Statue of [Rabih az-Zubayr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabih_az-Zubayr "Rabih az-Zubayr") at Maiduguri National Museum

The region was home to the [Kanem–Bornu Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanem%E2%80%93Bornu_Empire "Kanem–Bornu Empire") for centuries. Maiduguri actually consists of two cities: Yerwa to the West and Old Maiduguri to the east. Yerwa was founded in 1907 by [Abubakar Garbai of Borno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abubakar_Garbai_of_Borno "Abubakar Garbai of Borno") as the capital of the Bornu Kingdom.[[5]](#cite_note-Vincent-5) The location before that had been a small village known as Kalwa. This involved the transfer of the capital of the [Kanuri people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanuri_people "Kanuri people") from [Kukawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kukawa "Kukawa").

Old Maiduguri was selected by the British as their military headquarters in 1908, replacing [Mafoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mafoni?action=edit&redlink=1 "Mafoni (page does not exist)").[[3]](#cite_note-britannica-3) The same year it became the location for the British Resident Commissioner over British Bornu. In 1957, Yerwa became the designated name for the urban centre while 'Maiduguri' was officially applied as the name of the surrounding rural area. In 1964 the railway was extended here which led to its rise as a major commercial center in the region.

The city was once known as a "hub of Islamic scholarship in West Africa that ... [taught] tolerance and hospitality like its welcoming [neem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azadirachta_indica "Azadirachta indica") trees."[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Maiduguri is one of the fifteen Local Government Areas (LGAs) that constitute the [Borno Emirate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borno_Emirate "Borno Emirate"), a [traditional state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_traditional_states "Nigerian traditional states") located in Borno State, Nigeria.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

The **Blue Line** is an electric [rapid transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_transit "Rapid transit") line that runs in [Lagos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagos "Lagos"), [Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria "Nigeria").[[1]](#cite_note-time-1) It is part of the [Lagos Rail Mass Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagos_Rail_Mass_Transit "Lagos Rail Mass Transit") system run by the [Lagos Metropolitan Area Transport Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagos_Metropolitan_Area_Transport_Authority "Lagos Metropolitan Area Transport Authority").

The first phase with five stations and 13 kilometres (8.1 mi) of track opened on 4 September 2023.[[2]](#cite_note-2) The full line is set to be 27 kilometres (17 mi) and is expected to carry 500,000 passengers a day.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

The line's Class 210 trains are made by [CRRC Dalian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CRRC_Dalian "CRRC Dalian") and based on Chinese Type B trains from [Tianjin Metro Line 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_2_(Tianjin_Metro) "Line 2 (Tianjin Metro)"). They have a maximum speed of 100 [km/h](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilometres_per_hour "Kilometres per hour") (62 [mph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_per_hour "Miles per hour")), although they will only operate at 80 km/h (50 mph).[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Contents of https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/nigeria:
Former Governor of Lagos State Bola Ahmed Tinubu emerged as the winner of Nigeria’s closely watched February 2023 presidential election. Despite [repeated calls](https://www.hrw.org/news/2023/02/06/nigeria-impunity-insecurity-threaten-elections) to Nigerian authorities to prioritize accountability for [past elections-related abuses](https://www.hrw.org/news/2019/06/10/nigeria-widespread-violence-ushers-presidents-new-term) and address [widespread insecurity](https://www.hrw.org/news/2022/08/09/nigeria-insecurity-grips-nations-capital), the February elections were blighted by incidents of logistical failures and violence at the polls.

Multiple armed groups continue to kill and jeopardize the livelihood of millions across the country. In the Northwest, gangs of so-called bandits carry out widespread killings, kidnappings, sexual violence, and lootings, while in the Northeast, there has been a resurgence of attacks by the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), a breakout faction of Boko Haram.

Decades long intercommunal conflict between farmers and herders in the Middle Belt and Northcentral region continue to claim lives, while the authorities struggle to contain the clashes around land and other resources, which are exacerbated by ethnic and religious tensions.

In their responses to the security crisis across the country, security forces continue to be implicated in gross human rights abuses, including indiscriminate airstrikes, while the authorities have repeatedly failed to hold officers responsible for the abuses accountable through the justice system.

High rates of inflation due to the removal of a subsidy on petrol, among other factors, gave rise to an increase in multidimensional poverty and economic inequality. The high inflation rate undermined access to food and other necessities in a country where millions live in extreme poverty without a functional social protection system.

## Election-Related Violence

According to the Center for Democracy and Development, a nongovernmental organization (NGO), [a total of 109 election-related deaths were recorded across Nigeria in the build-up to the 2023 general election](https://www.premiumtimesng.com/news/top-news/588325-nigeria-recorded-109-deaths-in-three-months-linked-to-2023-elections-cdd.html)s.

The presidential and federal legislative elections [recorded several incidences of violence at the polls](https://www.hrw.org/news/2023/02/27/nigerias-elections-remain-risky-many-citizens), especially in battleground states like Lagos. Voters were exposed to violence by people referred to as “thugs” acting for, or on, behalf of politicians and political parties.

In some cases, voters were injured and stripped of their right to vote without any intervention from security forces.

## Violence in the Northwest and Northcentral Regions

In the Northwest, armed gangs of “bandits” continue to carry out widespread killings, kidnappings, sexual violence, and lootings. In February, a bloody confrontation between local vigilantes and bandits led to the killing of over 100 people in Katsina State. In April, [at least 80 people](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/gunmen-kidnap-80-including-children-northwest-nigeria-2023-04-08/), mostly women and children, were kidnapped by bandit gangs in Zamfara State. In July, [a video surfaced online](https://dailypost.ng/2023/07/23/bandits-threaten-to-marry-out-4-kidnapped-victims-in-zamfara/) where four female college students, whom they had abducted six months earlier, begged the government to pay their ransom so they would not be married off by the bandits.

Intercommunal violence between farmers and herders in the Northcentral region also recorded a high number of deaths. In May, over 100 people were killed in Plateau State. The violence was [reportedly in reprisal](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2023/5/19/more-than-100-people-dead-in-communal-clashes-in-central-nigeria) for farmers killing a herder after he and his cattle had encroached on their land.

A March[report by the International Organization for Migration (IOM)](https://dtm.iom.int/reports/nigeria-north-central-and-north-west-displacement-report-11-march-2023)documented a total of 1,190,293 internally displaced people in 191,688 households across the 8 states in the Northcentral and Northwest regions because of violence.

## Separatist Agitations in the Southeast Region

An ad hoc committee of the House of Representatives investigating communal clashes in Abia State [called for the release of Nnamdi Kanu](https://www.premiumtimesng.com/news/top-news/617616-reps-panel-says-release-of-ipob-leader-nnamdi-kanu-needed-for-peace-in-south-east.html), the leader of the Indigenous People of Biafra (IPOB), a group agitating for the secession of the Southeast region. Kanu was discharged and acquitted of treason and terrorism-related charges by Nigeria’s Court of Appeal, but he remains in custody following [a further appeal to the Supreme Court](https://dailypost.ng/2022

Contents of https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/nigeria:
/10/21/appeal-court-judgement-fg-drags-nnamdi-kanu-to-supreme-court/) by the federal government to challenge this decision.

States in the Southeast sought to put an end to the “sit at home order,” introduced by IPOB in 2021, which required citizens in the region to stay at home and for public places to stay closed on Mondays and any other day that is announced, including days Kanu is set to appear in court. Although IPOB says it has suspended the order, gunmen seeking to enforce it continue to kill, maim, and destroy properties of citizens in the region who defy it.

In Enugu, the state government [sealed some commercial banks and shops](https://www.channelstv.com/2023/07/24/enugu-govt-seals-shops-observing-ipob-sit-at-home-order/) for allegedly observing the Monday sit-at-home order.

## Boko Haram Conflict

Communities in Borno State, the epicenter of the Boko Haram conflict, witnessed a resurgence in attacks and kidnappings by armed groups. In March, over [30 fishermen and farmers were gruesomely killed](https://sunnewsonline.com/the-killing-of-30-borno-fishermen/) in an attack in Ngala Local Government Area. In June, [about 36 people](https://dailytrust.com/farmers-on-the-run-as-b-haram-killings-return/), including farmers, were killed in Dambo, Jere, and Mafa Local Government Areas.

According to [a media report](https://dailytrust.com/farmers-on-the-run-as-b-haram-killings-return/), ISWAP, a prominent breakout faction of Boko Haram, imposed a ban on farming, fishing, and herding activities in Marte Local Government Area. The move to halt agricultural activities was apparently to punish the farming communities for spying on them for the military, which carried out aerial bombardment against ISWAP.

## Abuses by Security Forces

In January, an [erroneous military airstrike in Nasarawa State](https://www.hrw.org/news/2023/06/06/nigeria-no-justice-civilians-killed-airstrike) killed 39 people and injured 6 others. Since 2017, [over 300 people are reported to have been killed by airstrikes](https://www.sbmintel.com/2023/02/chart-of-the-week-nigeria-air-force-mishaps/) that the Nigerian air force claimed were intended for bandits or members of Boko Haram and its breakout factions but instead hit civilians. In 2022, [the Nigerian air force announced an investigation into accidental airstrikes on civilian](https://www.premiumtimesng.com/news/headlines/562027-were-investigating-accidental-airstrikes-on-civilians-nigerian-air-force-chief.html)s but provided no further details.

In July, anti-police brutality [protests erupted in Anambra State, following the death of Chidubem Ezenwa in](https://businessday.ng/columnist/article/the-police-could-trigger-another-unrest-in-nigeria/) [police custody](https://dailypost.ng/2023/08/06/anambra-family-agonizes-over-sons-death-in-police-custody/), after allegedly being beaten by police operatives and other inmates. [Police said](https://dailypost.ng/2023/08/06/anambra-family-agonizes-over-sons-death-in-police-custody/) the inmates who beat him up have been arraigned for murder.

## Accountability for Serious Crimes

In February, the National Human Rights Commission began an investigation into allegations of [forced abortions](https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/nigeria-military-abortions/) and [infanticide](https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/nigeria-military-children/) in the Northeast Boko Haram conflict, but it has yet to produce its findings.

Domestic trials for hundreds of Boko Haram suspects have remained postponed since 2018.

The International Criminal Court (ICC) Office of the Prosecutor continued to consider whether to open an investigation into serious crimes committed in Nigeria and [indicated plans](https://asp.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/asp_docs/ICC-ASP-22-10-ENG-PPB-2024-31jul23-1500.pdf) to decide in 2024.

## Freedom of Expression and Media

In May, a Nigerian Court [found](https://punchng.com/just-in-nbc-has-no-powers-to-fine-broadcast-stations-court-rules/) that the National Broadcasting Commission (NBC), the country’s broadcast regulator, has no power to impose fines on broadcast stations. In April, NBC had fined [Channels Television 5 million](https://www.premiumtimesng.com/news/top-news/591249-nbc-fines-channels-tv-n5-million-over-dattis-ending-democracy-comment.html#:~:text=The%20National%20Broadcasting%20Code%20(NBC,Balarabe%20Ilelah%2C%20on%2027%20March.) Nigerian naira (about US$6,500) for allegedly violating the NBC code in a program during which a vice presidential candidate called on the authorities not to swear in Bola Tinubu.

Although the Nigerian Constitution guarantees the right to freedom of expression, thought, and conscience, insult to religion remains a criminal offense and Sharia (Islamic law), applicable in 12 northern states, criminalizes blasphemy.

Blasphemy-related accusations and killings [remain a concern](https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2023/country-chapters/nigeria#22ee4c) in northern Nigeria. In June, [Usman Buda was attacked and killed by a mob](https://dailytrust.com/how-sokoto-famous-butcher-was-killed-over-alleged-blasphemy/) in Sokoto State for alleged blasphemy against the Prophet Mohammed.

## Poverty and Inequality

President Tinubu announced the [removal of an existing subsidy on fuel](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-65737846) during his inauguration in May, resulting in increases in the price of food and other basic necessities. The authorities did not put in any measures to cushion the impact of the petrol subsidy removal, leaving [many Nigerians struggling to meet the basic needs of themselves and their families](https://www.theafricareport.com/316288/nigeria-petrol-price-hike-fuels-suffering/).

[The ability of communities to fish and farm continues to be stunted by rampant oil spills](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2023/feb/02/nearly-14000-nigerians-take-shell-to-court-over-devastating-impact-of-pollution) while the costs to public health is worsened by oil pollution and the [ongoing practice of excessive gas flaring.](https://blogs.worldbank.org/developmenttalk/impact-gas-flaring-child-health-nigeria)

In August, President Tinubu announced a [$650 million package](https://www.voanews.com/a/nigeria-s-tinubu-announces-650-million-aid-package-after-subsidy-removal-/7207196.html) that included funds to allow for a review of the minimum wage; support for small and medium businesses; and the purchase of gas-powered buses to reduce the cost of transportation, among other things.

## Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

In August, police in Delta State arrested dozens for [allegedly participating in a gay wedding](https://www.hrw.org/news/2023/08/30/nigerian-police-arrest-dozens-alleged-gay-wedding) at a hotel. The police streamed on Facebook a public parade of the detainees in front of journalists, where they were interrogated regarding the accusations in violation of their rights to fair trial, dignity, and privacy.

A total of [69 people were remanded to prison](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/nigerian-court-remands-dozens-prison-over-alleged-gay-wedding-2023-09-04/) in connection with the incident and later [released on bail pending trial.](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/nigerian-court-frees-bail-dozens-arrested-over-alleged-gay-wedding-lawyer-2023-09-19/#:~:text=A%20court%20sitting%20in%20southern,court%2C%20lawyer%20Ochuko%20Ohimor%20said.)

In October, [76 people were arrested in Gombe State for allegedly attending a birthday party for gay people](https://edition.cnn.com/2023/10/24/africa/nigeria-paramilitary-raids-gay-party-intl/index.html). The arrests were conducted by the Nigerian Security and Civil Defense Corps, the country’s paramilitary agency, which also alleged that the organizers of the party planned to hold a same-sex wedding.

The [Same Sex Marriage Prohibition Act](https://www.refworld.org/pdfid/52f4d9cc4.pdf), 2013, punishes same-sex marriage and public displays of same-sex relationships with 14 and 10 years’ imprisonment, respectively. It also punishes establishing, supporting, and participating in gay organizations with 10 years in prison.

A 2016 Human Rights Watch [report](https://www.hrw.org/report/2016/10/20/tell-me-where-i-can-be-safe/impact-nigerias-same-sex-marriage-prohibition-act) found that, despite no evidence that anyone had been prosecuted or sentenced under the law by that time, the law had served to legitimize abuses against lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) people in Nigeria, including extortion, arbitrary arrest, torture, and physical and sexual violence.

The police used the law for the first time in 2019 to [prosecute 47 men accused of same-sex public displays of affection](https://www.cnn.com/2019/12/12/africa/nigeria-men-trial-anti-gay-law-intl/index.html) in Lagos State. A court [dismissed](https://www.nytimes.com/2020/10/27/world/africa/Nigeria-anti-gay-law.html) the case because the police failed to appear and present witnesses.

## Women’s and Girl’s Rights

The outcomes of the 2023 elections in Nigeria have continued to raise concerns about the participation and representation of women in politics. [Women were elected to only 20 out of 469 federal legislative seats in the National Assembly](https://placng.org/Legist/worrying-numbers-for-women-in-10th-nass/), which comprises the Senate and the House of Representatives. This is a decline from the already abysmal number of 21 in the previous national elections.

A 2022 report by [Gender Strategy Advancement International](https://media.premiumtimesng.com/wp-content/files/2022/10/BASELINE-RESEARCH-ON-WOMENS-POLITICAL-PARTICIPATION-By-GSAI-1.pdf), a Nigerian NGO, highlights that although women make up [49 percent of Nigeria’s population, only 6.7 percent hold positions in government](https://media.premiumtimesng.com/wp-content/files/2022/10/BASELINE-RESEARCH-ON-WOMENS-POLITICAL-PARTICIPATION-By-GSAI-1.pdf), as women continue to suffer injustices and marginalization resulting from laws, religious and cultural norms, gender stereotypes, and low levels of education, among other things.

The [government has yet to adopt proposed amendments](https://guardian.ng/guardian-woman/women-seek-passage-of-gender-bills-ahead-of-10th-assembly/) to the country’s constitution, aimed at fostering women’s equality and participation in politics and government leadership, including through affirmative action.

Nigeria continued to have one of the [highest rates of maternal mortality in the world](https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/367617/9789240073678-eng.pdf?sequence=1), attributable to inadequate and unequitable access to maternal health care and a lack of access to safe and legal abortion. Nigeria also has one of the world’s highest rates of child marriage because of poor enforcement of national and state laws.

## Disability Rights

In January, then-President Muhammadu Buhari signed the Mental Health Bill into law, replacing the 1958 Lunacy Act. The new bill established some protections for people with mental health conditions, including the right to participate in their treatment plans. It also imposes a ban on chaining people with mental health conditions and aims to expand community-based coverage so more people can access mental health services. Contrary to international human rights standards, the law continues to permit involuntary treatment and allows coercion in other forms, including restraints and seclusion.

[Thousands of people with mental health conditions or psychosocial disabilities in Nigeria continue to be shackled](https://www.hrw.org/news/2019/11/11/nigeria-people-mental-health-conditions-chained-abused), chained, and locked in confined spaces in various facilities across the country, including in some traditional and religious healing centers, state-run rehabilitation centers, and even in some psychiatric hospitals.

Contents of https://www.voanews.com/a/nigeria-s-tinubu-announces-650-million-aid-package-after-subsidy-removal-/7207196.html:
Abuja, Nigeria — 

Nigerian labor unions held meetings with the government Tuesday to discuss the removal of fuel subsidies that have led to increases in fuel prices and the threat of strikes. The meetings come a day after the president announced a $650 million financial package to assist households hurt by economic reforms.

During a televised address, President Bola Tinubu defended his decision to scrap the fuel subsidy, saying it only benefited a few so-called elites. Tinubu said he was aware of the hardships that the decision caused citizens and promised his government was working to help.

The latest measures announced by the president include allocations for a review of the minimum wage, support for micro-, small- and medium-scale enterprises, and the purchase of 3,000 gas-powered buses to reduce the cost of transportation.

Tinubu also ordered the immediate release of 200,000 metric tons of grains to households, in an effort to lower prices, and 225,000 metric tons of fertilizers, seedlings and other inputs to farmers.

"I had promised to reform the economy for the long-term good by fighting major imbalances that have plagued our economy," Tinubu said. "Ending the subsidy and preferential exchange rate system were key to this fight. This fight is to define the fate and future of our nation."

Upon assuming office in late May, Tinubu embarked on some of Nigeria's biggest reforms in decades, including floating of the country's currency, the naira.

Fuel prices have more than tripled since the subsidy removal and the currency has weakened against the U.S. dollar. The developments increased pressure on the government to ease the suffering caused by the policies.

Authorities say the decision will pay off in the long run. On Monday, Tinubu said the country has saved $1.32 billion since scrapping the subsidy in late May.

"Such a vast sum of money would have been better spent on public transportation, health care, schools, housing and even national security," he said.

But economist Isaac Botti said authorities should have implemented measures in advance to cushion the effect of removing the subsidy.

"What the government ought to have done was to create the shock absorber, but trying to salvage a crisis after it has occurred for me is an afterthought," Botti said. "So what the president expressed in his speech were things he should have done or should have been out in place before the pronouncement of subsidy removal."

Botti said Nigeria needs to consider local refining of oil if it is going to bring down soaring fuel prices.

"What is the plan [including] short, medium and long term to address the issue of refining petrol in this country? Whatever measures the government is bringing on board should be able to address the realities on ground," he said.

Last month, Tinubu announced plans to transfer $10 million to $12 million to poor households in a bid to ease the impact of the subsidy removal.

Meanwhile, the labor unions met with government officials hoping to reach an agreement that will prevent workers from holding a planned protest on Wednesday.

***The Lion of Bourdillon*** is a 2015 [documentary film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Documentary_film "Documentary film") aired by [Africa Independent Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa_Independent_Television "Africa Independent Television"), a Nigerian Television Station popularly known as AIT.[[1]](#cite_note-1)
The film centers on the political life of Senator [Bola Tinubu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bola_Tinubu "Bola Tinubu"), the former [Lagos State Governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagos_State_Governor "Lagos State Governor") and the National leader of the [All Progressives Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Progressives_Congress "All Progressives Congress").[[2]](#cite_note-2)
It was first aired on March 1, 2015, but then stopped from further airing on March 6, 2015, following a N150 billion libel suit filled by Tinubu against AIT.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

## Controversies and criticisms

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=The_Lion_of_Bourdillon&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Controversies and criticisms")]

The airing of the documentary film on March 1, 2015, generated several controversies, leading to a N150 billion libel suit against AIT by Bola Tinubu.[[4]](#cite_note-4)
The hour-long documentary film revealed the personal life of the former governor, showing him participating in a certain level of corruption during and after his tenure in office as governor of [Lagos State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagos_State "Lagos State"). It revealed properties and companies owned by the Senator across Lagos State, describing him as "Nigeria's biggest landlord".[[5]](#cite_note-5) The film also revealed that he was charged for [drug trafficking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_trafficking "Drug trafficking") in 1993 by the [United States government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_government "United States government").

The film's release was described by critics as an attempt to tarnish Tinubu's image as a leader of a ruling party, the [All Progressives Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Progressives_Congress "All Progressives Congress").[[6]](#cite_note-6)
[Abimbola Adelakun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abimbola_Adelakun "Abimbola Adelakun"), a Nigerian writer and columnist of *[The Punch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Punch "The Punch")*, strongly criticized the film's release in her publications on March 5, 2015, describing the airing of the film as "libelous and defamatory", accusing the [People's Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Democratic_Party_(Nigeria) "People's Democratic Party (Nigeria)") of being an accomplice.[[7]](#cite_note-7) In the same vein, the Nigerian lawmaker [Michael Opeyemi Bamidele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Opeyemi_Bamidele "Michael Opeyemi Bamidele") wrote an article entitled "My hatred for Asiwaju Bola Tinubu", in which he criticized the documentary film and the opposition party's role in its release.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

On March 6, 2015, [Bola Tinubu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bola_Tinubu "Bola Tinubu") instituted a N150 billion suit against AIT on alleged [defamation of character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defamation "Defamation").[[9]](#cite_note-9)
Bola Tinubu claimed that the documentary film was politically sponsored in order to tarnish his reputation.
Justice Akinkugbe of the [High Court of Lagos State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Court_of_Lagos_State "High Court of Lagos State") presided over the case.[[10]](#cite_note-10)
On April 1, 2015, the court restrained the AIT from further airing of the controversial documentary pending the outcome of the suit.[[11]](#cite_note-11)
AIT, in a counter claim made through its chairman, [Raymond Dokpesi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raymond_Dokpesi "Raymond Dokpesi"), speaking under oath, refuted the claim by the Senator, saying that the film was not designed to attack his personality or aired out of malice.[[12]](#cite_note-12)
He emphasized that the broadcasting station was empowered and entrusted by Section 22 of the [Constitution of Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Nigeria "Constitution of Nigeria") to hold those in government accountable and responsible to [Nigerians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerians "Nigerians").[[13]](#cite_note-13)

The **Economic and Financial Crimes Commission** (**EFCC**) is a [Nigerian](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerians "Nigerians") law enforcement and anti-graft agency that investigates financial crimes and unknown transactions such as [advance fee fraud](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advance_fee_fraud "Advance fee fraud") (419 fraud) and [money laundering](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Money_laundering "Money laundering").[[1]](#cite_note-establishment-1) The EFCC was established in 2003, partially in response to pressure from the [Financial Action Task Force on Money Laundering](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_Action_Task_Force_on_Money_Laundering "Financial Action Task Force on Money Laundering") (FATF),[[2]](#cite_note-2) which named Nigeria as one of 23 countries non-cooperative in the international community's efforts to fight money laundering.[[1]](#cite_note-establishment-1) The agency has its head office in [Abuja](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abuja "Abuja"), Nigeria. The EFCC was also set up to fight against corruption and protect the country from economic saboteurs. The current [chairman of EFCC](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairman_of_the_EFCC "Chairman of the EFCC") is [Ola Olukoyede](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olanipekun_Olukayode "Olanipekun Olukayode"), appointed by President [Bola Tinubu](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bola_Tinubu "Bola Tinubu") on 12 October 2023.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) was established on December 12, 2002, by President [Olusegun Obasanjo](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olusegun_Obasanjo "Olusegun Obasanjo")'s administration to combat financial crimes and money laundering. The commission's creation was partly in response to pressure from the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) on Money Laundering, which had ranked Nigeria as one of 23 non-cooperative countries. However, on April 13, 2003, the EFCC commenced operational activities under [Nuhu Ribadu](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuhu_Ribadu "Nuhu Ribadu") as the pioneer Executive Chairman. Under [Nuhu Ribadu](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuhu_Ribadu "Nuhu Ribadu"), the agency addressed financial [corruption](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corruption "Corruption") by prosecuting and convicting a number of high-profile corrupt individuals, ranging from Nigeria's former chief law enforcement officer to several bank chief executives. Contents of https://www.voanews.com/a/many-feared-dead-as-nigerian-military-airstrike-hits-local-village-/7384126.html:
abuja, nigeria — 

Nigerian authorities said Monday that a military airstrike targeting terrorists in northern Kaduna state had erroneously hit a local village and killed civilians there.

Officials of the Kaduna state Ministry of Internal Security and Home Affairs confirmed the incident after an emergency security meeting Monday.

Authorities said the military jet was on a routine counterterrorism operation Sunday when it inadvertently bombed the Tudun village in the state and killed dozens of residents.

The victims had gathered to mark the Maulud celebration, the birthday of the Prophet Muhammad that night, when the incident occurred.

Authorities did not give details on casualties but local media reported at least 30 people were killed, and dozens of others were being treated in the hospital.

The state government said Monday that search-and-rescue operations were still underway.

Mike Medubi, media aide to the Kaduna state security commissioner, told VOA by phone, "The official statement is the only authoritative source right now, as no numbers have been published or released from the end of the Kaduna state government. ... I don't know where the other media sources are getting their numbers from."

The Kaduna state government sent condolences to the affected families.

This wasn't the first time this year that a military airstrike had killed civilians in Nigeria.

In January, an airstrike hit a small settlement in Nasarawa state near Abuja, killing 39 people and injuring six others.

Civilian casualties during military operations have in the past sparked debate about such operations as well as war accountability in Nigeria.

Nigeria has been struggling to end a 14-year Islamic insurgency in its northeast and keep armed gangs from spreading across the northwest and central states.

Kaduna is one of the states affected by the activities of kidnap-for-ransom gangs.
